meta.blurb: Legend says a border guard begged an old sage to write down his wisdom before he left China. What he left were eighty-one short poems about water, silence and a strength that does not push. Short enough to read in an evening.
meta.bible: Tao Te Ching: a short book of 81 brief chapters from ancient China; the title can be translated as the Way and its Power. Laozi: the sage to whom tradition gives the book; the name means Old Master. Historians cannot say for certain who he was, whether he was one person or several, or exactly when the text was put together; the old story that he wrote it for a gatekeeper at the western pass as he left China is a legend. Tao: the Way, the deep pattern behind all things. Te: power or virtue. China: the ancient country where the book was written. The sage: the wise person the book describes, who acts without forcing, does not boast and does not hoard. Ten thousand things: the old way of saying everything in the world. Heaven: the great natural order above. The book has 200 beats in 20 groups of ten. Beat 1 introduces the book and Laozi; beats 2 to 199 follow the 81 chapters of the Tao Te Ching in their own order, each chapter taking one to four beats and named in the text by its ordinal (the first chapter, the twenty-fifth chapter); beat 200 tells the legend of Laozi and the gatekeeper and ends the book. Chapters 1 to 37 are the first half (the Way) and chapters 38 to 81 the second half (virtue, Te). Fixed facts used: the book has about five thousand written characters; the oldest copies were buried in tombs; a straw dog was a ceremonial offering used once and thrown away; yin and yang are the dark and the light; the Mother and the Mysterious Female are names for the Tao; the One is the unity of the Tao; the Uncarved Block is plain wood, the picture of simplicity; the three treasures are compassion, frugality and not daring to be first; Heaven's Net is the wide net that misses nothing. Socrates, the Greek philosopher, is named once as a comparison and nothing is claimed about any link. Where translators read a passage differently (chapter 50's numbers, chapter 39's carriage, chapter 65's simple people) the text says so. Voice and tone: calm, plain, gentle and slightly humorous; the chapters are paraphrased and never copied; respectful of the tradition and neutral; nothing preached; no gore.

beats.scene: An old man in plain robes rides an ox toward a mountain pass
beats.summary: Introduces the Tao Te Ching, its 81 short chapters, and the sage Laozi, whom tradition names as its author.

beats.scene: A mountain peak is lost in mist above a quiet river
beats.summary: Chapter 1: the Tao that can be put into words is not the lasting Tao.

beats.scene: A bare hilltop at dawn, with a valley full of small houses below
beats.summary: Chapter 1: the nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth, and the named is the mother of all things.

beats.scene: A pair of open wooden gates standing in morning light
beats.summary: Chapter 1: without desire one sees the mystery, with desire only the surface; both come from one source, the gate of all wonders.

beats.scene: A tall tree and a small flower grow side by side
beats.summary: Chapter 2: beauty and ugliness, long and short, high and low depend on each other.

beats.scene: A quiet old man tends a garden and walks away unthanked
beats.summary: Chapter 2: the sage acts without forcing and teaches without speeches.

beats.scene: Seedlings push up through soil while a gardener walks away
beats.summary: Chapter 2: the sage lets things grow, makes without owning, finishes without clinging, and so the work lasts.

beats.scene: A quiet village where a small jewelled box sits unguarded on a table
beats.summary: Chapter 3: if talent is not praised and rare treasures are not prized, people stop competing and stealing.

beats.scene: A baker hands round warm loaves to a calm, smiling crowd
beats.summary: Chapter 3: the sage empties hearts of craving, fills bellies and strengthens bones; with no forcing, nothing is left in disorder.

beats.scene: A plain empty bowl on a table, with a soft light falling into it
beats.summary: Chapter 4: the Tao is like an empty bowl that is never filled; it softens sharp edges, unties knots and blends with the dust.

beats.scene: Rain falls evenly on a farm, a forest and a city
beats.summary: Chapter 5: heaven and earth are impartial and treat all things like straw dogs, and the sage treats people the same way.

beats.scene: A blacksmith's leather bellows puffing air into a glowing fire
beats.summary: Chapter 5: the space between heaven and earth is like a bellows, empty yet never exhausted; too many words wear one out, so hold to the centre.

beats.scene: A deep green valley with a stream running quietly through its centre
beats.summary: Chapter 6: the valley spirit never dies and is called the mysterious female.

beats.scene: Mist drifts out of a narrow cave mouth in a green hillside
beats.summary: Chapter 6: the gate of the mysterious female is the root of heaven and earth; it seems to be always present and is never used up.

beats.scene: The sun rises over a wide sea while waves roll gently
beats.summary: Chapter 7: heaven and earth last long because they do not live for themselves.

beats.scene: A traveller steps aside to let a long line of people pass first
beats.summary: Chapter 7: the sage puts himself last and finds himself in front; he stays outside and is kept safe.

beats.scene: Neighbours gather round a modest man and ask him to lead
beats.summary: Chapter 7: because he wants nothing for himself, the sage's own needs are met.

beats.scene: A stream flows around smooth stones toward the sea
beats.summary: Chapter 8: the highest good is like water, which helps all things and competes with none.

beats.scene: Rain gathers in a muddy hollow while people walk on the high road
beats.summary: Chapter 8: water settles in the low places that people avoid, and so it is close to the Tao.

beats.scene: A man stands calmly in a field at sunrise, handing seed to a neighbour
beats.summary: Chapter 8: the good person lives, thinks, gives, speaks, rules and acts well, and because he does not compete he is never blamed.

beats.scene: A bowl filled to the very edge, with water about to spill over
beats.summary: Chapter 9: a bowl filled too full spills, and a blade sharpened too much will not last.

beats.scene: A hall piled with gold and jade, with one worried guard
beats.summary: Chapter 9: no one can guard a hall full of gold and jade, and pride in riches brings trouble; when the work is done, step back.

beats.scene: A baby asleep in a cradle, breathing softly
beats.summary: Chapter 10: can you keep body and spirit together and breathe as softly as a baby?

beats.scene: A woman gently wipes dust from a dark bronze mirror
beats.summary: Chapter 10: can you clean the mirror of the mind until it has no flaw, and love the people and rule without cleverness?

beats.scene: A mother hen leads her chicks across a farmyard without herding them
beats.summary: Chapter 10: to give birth and nourish, to make without owning, to act without expecting thanks and to lead without controlling is the mysterious virtue.

beats.scene: A cartwheel with thirty spokes meeting at its hollow hub
beats.summary: Chapter 11: thirty spokes meet at a hub, and it is the empty space in the middle that makes the wheel useful.

beats.scene: A potter shapes a clay bowl on a spinning wheel
beats.summary: Chapter 11: a potter shapes clay into a pot, and the hollow inside is what makes it useful.

beats.scene: Sunlight pours through a window into a bare, empty room
beats.summary: Chapter 11: doors and windows are cut to make a room, and the empty space is what is used; what is there gives benefit, what is not there gives use.

beats.scene: A busy market stall of bright cloth, loud drums and spicy food
beats.summary: Chapter 12: the five colours blind the eye, the five sounds deafen the ear and the five flavours dull the taste.

beats.scene: Horsemen gallop across a field while a quiet man eats a simple meal
beats.summary: Chapter 12: racing and hunting unsettle the mind and rare goods lead people astray, so the sage cares about real needs and not show.

beats.scene: A court official bows nervously before a throne as a crowd watches
beats.summary: Chapter 13: favour and disgrace both shake a person, because both depend on what others think.

beats.scene: A ruler looks out over a village as though it were his own family
beats.summary: Chapter 13: we suffer because we think so much of ourselves; one who values the world as he values himself can be trusted with it.

beats.scene: A hand reaches toward morning mist and closes on empty air
beats.summary: Chapter 14: the Tao cannot be seen, heard or grasped, and the three are really one.

beats.scene: Grey hills where earth and sky blur together in the mist
beats.summary: Chapter 14: the Tao is not bright above or dark below; it has no name, and it returns to nothing, a shape without a shape.

beats.scene: A traveller follows a long thread across a quiet green hillside
beats.summary: Chapter 14: meet it and it has no front, follow it and it has no back; holding the ancient Way one can manage the present.

beats.scene: A man picks his way across a frozen winter stream
beats.summary: Chapter 15: the old masters were too deep to understand, so the writer describes them: careful as a man crossing a winter stream, alert as one with danger around.

beats.scene: A guest bows politely at a gate beside a thawing pond
beats.summary: Chapter 15: they were polite as guests, yielding like melting ice, plain as uncut wood, open as a valley and cloudy as muddy water.

beats.scene: Muddy water in a glass jar slowly settles and turns clear
beats.summary: Chapter 15: muddy water becomes clear if left still, and a still thing can be stirred slowly into life; those who follow the Tao do not seek to be full, so they can always renew themselves.

beats.scene: Bare winter trees whose fallen leaves return quietly to the soil
beats.summary: Chapter 16: reach emptiness, keep stillness; the ten thousand things rise and flourish and each returns to its root.

beats.scene: An old man sits peacefully at the foot of a great tree at dusk
beats.summary: Chapter 16: returning to the root is stillness; to know this constancy is to be wise and open-minded, and then the body can perish without danger.

beats.scene: Villagers work a field while their ruler watches from far away
beats.summary: Chapter 17: the best ruler is hardly known to his people; next comes one who is loved and praised, then one who is feared, then one who is despised.

beats.scene: Farmers harvest together, laughing, and say they did it themselves
beats.summary: Chapter 17: where trust is lacking there is distrust; a good ruler speaks little, and when the work is done his people say they did it themselves.

beats.scene: A man carries a banner about goodness while neighbours look doubtful
beats.summary: Chapter 18: when the great Way is lost, kindness and duty appear, and when cleverness arises, there is great pretending.

beats.scene: A family argues at a table while a loyal servant stands by
beats.summary: Chapter 18: when a family is not at peace, dutiful sons appear, and when a state is in chaos, loyal ministers appear.

beats.scene: A tangled knot of fancy rope lies discarded in the road
beats.summary: Chapter 19: if cleverness and showy wisdom were given up, people would gain a hundredfold; if showy kindness and duty were given up, they would return to natural love.

beats.scene: A simple bolt of plain undyed cloth lies on a wooden table
beats.summary: Chapter 19: give up skill and profit and there will be no thieves; hold to plain silk, uncarved wood, few wishes and little self-interest.

beats.scene: A crowd feasts on a hilltop terrace while one man sits apart
beats.summary: Chapter 20: give up learning and there is no worry; others feast as if at a spring festival, while the writer drifts alone like a baby who has not yet smiled.

beats.scene: A lone traveller with an empty bag stands at a crossroads
beats.summary: Chapter 20: the writer feels tired and homeless, while others have more than enough; he has the mind of a fool, all muddled.

beats.scene: A small boat drifts on a wide calm sea with no shore in sight
beats.summary: Chapter 20: ordinary people are bright and sharp, but the writer is dim and dull, calm as the sea and drifting without a place to stop.

beats.scene: A small calf drinks from its mother in a quiet meadow
beats.summary: Chapter 20: everyone has a purpose, but the writer is stubborn and rustic; he differs from them in valuing nourishment from the Mother, the Way.

beats.scene: A faint glow of light inside a dark, still cave
beats.summary: Chapter 21: great virtue follows the Tao alone; the Tao is vague and elusive, yet inside it are images, things and a pure essence.

beats.scene: An old carved stone with a name worn smooth by wind and rain
beats.summary: Chapter 21: this essence is real, its name has never gone away, and through it the writer sees how all things begin.

beats.scene: A bamboo stalk bends in a strong wind and then stands straight again
beats.summary: Chapter 22: what bends becomes whole, what is crooked becomes straight, what is hollow is filled; with little one gains, with much one is confused.

beats.scene: A modest man stands quietly in a doorway while others push to the front
beats.summary: Chapter 22: the sage embraces the One and is a model for the world; because he does not display himself he shines, and because he does not justify himself he is respected.

beats.scene: A finished wooden chair stands in a workshop with no sign of its maker
beats.summary: Chapter 22: he does not boast, so he has merit; he does not brag, so he lasts; because he does not compete, nobody can compete with him; to yield is to remain whole.

beats.scene: A violent storm passes and the sun returns over wet fields
beats.summary: Chapter 23: to speak little is natural; a whirlwind does not last all morning and a downpour does not last all day.

beats.scene: Three travellers walk three different paths from a fork in the road
beats.summary: Chapter 23: if heaven and earth cannot make things last by force, neither can people; those who follow the Tao become one with the Tao, and those who lack trust will not be trusted.

beats.scene: A man on tiptoe stretches high and wobbles beside a steady walker
beats.summary: Chapter 24: one who stands on tiptoe cannot stand firmly, and one who strides cannot walk far.

beats.scene: A loud man waves his arms and boasts while villagers walk away
beats.summary: Chapter 24: one who shows himself off is not bright, one who justifies himself is not distinguished, and one who boasts or brags will not last.

beats.scene: A heap of leftover scraps and a stuffed bag lie by the road
beats.summary: Chapter 24: to the Tao these habits are like leftover food and extra baggage that everyone dislikes, so a person who has the Tao does not dwell on them.

beats.scene: A glowing circle of mist hangs above a still dark sea before dawn
beats.summary: Chapter 25: something silent and whole existed before heaven and earth; it stands alone, does not change, and may be the mother of the world.

beats.scene: A great ring of birds flies out over the hills and curves back
beats.summary: Chapter 25: the writer does not know its name and calls it the Tao, or if he must, the Great; to be great is to go on, to go far, and to return.

beats.scene: A man, a field, the sky and a ring of light in a row
beats.summary: Chapter 25: the Tao, heaven, earth and the king are all great; people follow the earth, the earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Tao, and the Tao follows what is natural.

beats.scene: A traveller walks beside a heavily loaded wagon along a long road
beats.summary: Chapter 26: the heavy is the root of the light and stillness is the master of restlessness, so the sage never leaves his baggage wagon when travelling.

beats.scene: A king hurries by in a golden chariot, scattering startled birds
beats.summary: Chapter 26: although he sees splendid sights, the sage stays calm; a ruler who treats himself lightly loses his root, and one who is restless loses his command.

beats.scene: Footprints are missing from fresh snow behind a quiet traveller
beats.summary: Chapter 27: a good traveller leaves no tracks, a good speaker makes no mistakes, a good counter needs no tally, and a good door needs no bolt.

beats.scene: A gardener lifts a fallen seedling and replants it gently
beats.summary: Chapter 27: the sage is good at helping people, so nobody is abandoned, and good at saving things, so nothing is wasted; this is called following the light.

beats.scene: A craftsman shows a young apprentice a rough block of wood
beats.summary: Chapter 27: the good person is the teacher of the not-good, and the not-good is the material of the good; not to value the teacher nor love the material is to be greatly lost.

beats.scene: A broad valley holds a quiet stream while a child plays beside it
beats.summary: Chapter 28: know the strong and keep to the soft, be the valley of the world, and return to the state of a child.

beats.scene: A plain block of pale wood lies uncarved on a workbench
beats.summary: Chapter 28: return to the uncarved block; when it is cut it becomes tools, and the sage uses them to lead, but the greatest carving does not cut.

beats.scene: A man grips a delicate clay jar too hard and it cracks
beats.summary: Chapter 29: those who try to take the world and improve it by force will fail, because the world is a sacred vessel; those who act on it spoil it, and those who grasp it lose it.

beats.scene: People of many kinds walk the same road, some fast and some slow
beats.summary: Chapter 29: some lead and some follow, some are strong and some weak; so the sage avoids extremes, excess and extravagance.

beats.scene: Thorn bushes grow over an empty field where an army once camped
beats.summary: Chapter 30: one who serves a ruler by the Tao does not use weapons to force the world; where armies camp, thorns grow, and a great war is followed by years of bad harvest.

beats.scene: A soldier hangs his helmet on a peg beside a door
beats.summary: Chapter 30: a good commander achieves his result and stops; he does not boast or brag, and he acts only because he has no choice.

beats.scene: A strong young bull in a meadow beside a tired old bull
beats.summary: Chapter 30: when things reach their full strength they begin to age; this is against the Tao, and what is against the Tao ends early.

beats.scene: Swords and spears hang unused on a dusty wall
beats.summary: Chapter 31: weapons are tools of ill omen that people dislike, so one who follows the Tao does not make a home among them.

beats.scene: A general stands calmly with his hand on a sheathed sword
beats.summary: Chapter 31: weapons are not a gentleman's tools and should be used only when there is no choice; restraint is best, and a victory is nothing to admire.

beats.scene: A general lays down his sword and bows his head over a quiet field
beats.summary: Chapter 31: when many people have been killed, they should be mourned with sorrow, and a victory should be celebrated like a funeral.

beats.scene: Sweet morning dew shines on the grass of a peaceful field
beats.summary: Chapter 32: the Tao is always nameless, like an uncarved block; though small, nothing under heaven can master it, and if kings could hold it, all things would come to them of their own accord.

beats.scene: Small streams run down a hillside into a great river and the sea
beats.summary: Chapter 32: once the block is cut, names arrive, and one must know when to stop; the Tao in the world is like streams flowing into rivers and seas.

beats.scene: A man stands before a still pond and looks at his own reflection
beats.summary: Chapter 33: to know others is to be clever, but to know oneself is to be wise.

beats.scene: A wrestler wins a match and then sits alone in a quiet room
beats.summary: Chapter 33: to master others takes force, but to master oneself takes true strength.

beats.scene: An old man smiles at his modest home as the sun sets
beats.summary: Chapter 33: to know contentment is to be rich; one who does not lose his place endures, and one who dies but is not forgotten has a long life.

beats.scene: A broad river spreads into countless streams across a green plain
beats.summary: Chapter 34: the great Tao flows everywhere, left and right; all things depend on it for life and it turns none away, yet it claims no credit and does not rule over them.

beats.scene: A modest hillside spring feeds a wide plain of green fields below
beats.summary: Chapter 34: because it never tries to make itself great, the Tao is able to accomplish greatness.

beats.scene: Travellers stream toward a quiet village with one lit lantern
beats.summary: Chapter 35: hold to the great image and the world will come to you; they come without harm and find safety, peace and calm.

beats.scene: Travellers stop at a food stall while a plain teahouse stands empty
beats.summary: Chapter 35: music and good food make passing guests stop, but the Tao, when spoken, is bland and without flavour; it cannot be seen or heard, yet it cannot be used up.

beats.scene: A tall wave rises high on the sea, ready to fall
beats.summary: Chapter 36: to shrink something, first let it grow; to weaken something, first let it be strong; to take something, first give; this is subtle insight.

beats.scene: A thin green shoot pushes up through a heavy paving stone
beats.summary: Chapter 36: the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong.

beats.scene: A fish swims in deep dark water, far below the surface
beats.summary: Chapter 36: a fish should not leave the deep water, and a state's sharp weapons should not be shown to the people.

beats.scene: A king watches the fields grow by themselves under a bright sky
beats.summary: Chapter 37: the Tao does nothing, yet nothing is left undone.

beats.scene: A calm village at dusk with lamps lit and no guards at the gate
beats.summary: Chapter 37: if rulers could hold to the Tao, all things would change of their own accord; where desire arises, the nameless uncarved block calms it, and the world settles by itself.

beats.scene: A man quietly leaves a basket of bread at a neighbour's door
beats.summary: Chapter 38: high virtue is not aware of being virtuous, and so it has virtue; low virtue never forgets its goodness, and so it has none.

beats.scene: A staircase goes downward, each step lit by a dimmer lamp
beats.summary: Chapter 38: when the Way is lost there is virtue, then kindness, then duty, and then ritual, which is the thin edge of loyalty and the beginning of disorder.

beats.scene: A ripe fruit hangs on a branch beside a fading blossom
beats.summary: Chapter 38: foreknowledge is the flower of the Tao and the start of folly, so the great person chooses the solid fruit and not the flower.

beats.scene: A clear sky above steady ground and a full green valley
beats.summary: Chapter 39: in the beginning, certain things attained the One: heaven became clear, earth steady, spirits powerful, valleys full and rulers upright.

beats.scene: A great crack runs through dry ground beneath a cloudy sky
beats.summary: Chapter 39: without the One, heaven would crack, earth would split, spirits would lose their power, valleys would dry up and rulers would fall.

beats.scene: A cart wheel, axle and boards lie in pieces beside a road
beats.summary: Chapter 39: the high rests on the low and the noble on the humble; rulers call themselves lonely and unworthy, and a carriage counted into its parts is no carriage.

beats.scene: A ripple on a pond spreads outward and slowly returns to calm
beats.summary: Chapter 40: returning is the movement of the Tao, and yielding is the way it works.

beats.scene: A seed splits open in dark soil as a green shoot rises
beats.summary: Chapter 40: all things in the world are born from being, and being is born from non-being.

beats.scene: Three travellers hear a teaching: one nods, one doubts and one laughs aloud
beats.summary: Chapter 41: the best student hears the Tao and practises it, the middling student keeps it and loses it, and the lowest laughs out loud; without that laughter it would not be the Tao.

beats.scene: A steep path that looks like it goes down but leads up the mountain
beats.summary: Chapter 41: the bright Tao seems dark, the advancing Tao seems to retreat, the smooth Tao seems rough, and high virtue seems like a valley.

beats.scene: A great bell hums faintly in a vast, quiet hall
beats.summary: Chapter 41: the great square has no corners, the great vessel is slow to be finished, the great sound is faint and the great image has no shape; the Tao is hidden and nameless, yet it alone nourishes and completes all things.

beats.scene: One flame lights two lamps, then three, then a whole hall of lamps
beats.summary: Chapter 42: the Tao gave birth to one, one to two, two to three, and three to the ten thousand things.

beats.scene: A dark half and a light half of a circle turn together
beats.summary: Chapter 42: the ten thousand things carry the dark on their backs and embrace the light in their arms, and blending their breath they find harmony.

beats.scene: A king in plain clothes sits low among villagers on the ground
beats.summary: Chapter 42: people dislike being called lonely, orphaned or unworthy, yet kings use these names for themselves; things may gain by losing and lose by gaining.

beats.scene: Soft water wears a hollow in a hard grey stone
beats.summary: Chapter 43: the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest, and what has no substance can enter where there is no space.

beats.scene: A teacher sits in silence beside a student while a candle burns
beats.summary: Chapter 43: teaching without words and doing without forcing are of benefit, but few in the world can reach them.

beats.scene: A man weighs a bag of gold and a trophy on a balance
beats.summary: Chapter 44: fame or one's own self, which is dearer; one's own self or one's wealth, which matters more; gain or loss, which is the worse?

beats.scene: A woman holds a small bowl of rice beside a heap of gold
beats.summary: Chapter 44: great love brings great cost and great hoarding brings great loss; one who knows contentment is not disgraced, and one who knows when to stop is safe.

beats.scene: An old dented kettle still serves tea to a crowd
beats.summary: Chapter 45: great perfection seems flawed, yet its use never wears out, and great fullness seems empty, yet its use never runs dry.

beats.scene: A master carpenter's rough bench with a few plain, worn tools
beats.summary: Chapter 45: great straightness seems bent, great skill seems clumsy and great eloquence seems to stammer.

beats.scene: A man walks briskly through snow while another sits still in the shade
beats.summary: Chapter 45: movement overcomes cold and stillness overcomes heat; clarity and stillness set the standard for the world.

beats.scene: A farmer ploughs a field with a strong horse beside a peaceful village
beats.summary: Chapter 46: when the Tao is in the world, galloping horses are used to haul manure for the fields; when it is not, war horses are bred in the countryside.

beats.scene: A man sits content with a small cup of tea at sunset
beats.summary: Chapter 46: there is no greater calamity than not knowing contentment and no greater fault than the wish to acquire more; the contentment of knowing enough is always enough.

beats.scene: A man sits by a closed door and gazes out of a window
beats.summary: Chapter 47: one can know the world without going out of the door, and see the Way of heaven without looking out of the window.

beats.scene: A traveller hurries along a dusty road while a sage sits calmly at home
beats.summary: Chapter 47: the farther one goes, the less one knows; the sage knows without travelling, names without seeing and accomplishes without acting.

beats.scene: A scholar's desk heaped with books beside an empty, quiet garden
beats.summary: Chapter 48: in the pursuit of learning, something is gained every day; in the pursuit of the Tao, something is dropped every day.

beats.scene: A gardener rests under a tree while the garden grows around him
beats.summary: Chapter 48: dropping more and more, one reaches doing nothing, and when nothing is forced, nothing is left undone.

beats.scene: A ruler sits with folded hands while a market bustles around him
beats.summary: Chapter 48: the world is won by not meddling, and one who meddles is not fit to rule it.

beats.scene: An old man listens with an open face to a crowd of villagers
beats.summary: Chapter 49: the sage has no fixed mind of his own and takes the minds of the people as his own.

beats.scene: A wise old man shares his bread with two very different strangers
beats.summary: Chapter 49: the sage is good to those who are good and also to those who are not good, and he trusts both the trustworthy and the untrustworthy; that is the goodness of virtue.

beats.scene: A kind old man smiles at a ring of curious children
beats.summary: Chapter 49: the sage is cautious and blends his mind with the world; people keep their eyes and ears on him, and he treats them all as children.

beats.scene: A path splits toward a sunny meadow and a dark gate
beats.summary: Chapter 50: going out is life and coming in is death; some are followers of life, some of death, and some pass from life toward death by their own choices.

beats.scene: A man clutches a bag of gold tightly as he hurries along
beats.summary: Chapter 50: the reason is that they hold on to life too intensely.

beats.scene: A traveller walks calmly through a forest where a tiger rests
beats.summary: Chapter 50: one who knows how to hold on to life walks without fear of tigers or buffalo and goes through battle unharmed, because there is no place in him for death to enter.

beats.scene: A seedling grows in the sun and rain, serving no master
beats.summary: Chapter 51: the Tao gives birth to things, virtue nurtures them, the world shapes them and circumstance completes them; so all things honour the Tao and value virtue, not by command but naturally.

beats.scene: A mother bird shelters her chicks under her wing
beats.summary: Chapter 51: the Tao gives birth, nourishes, shelters and protects, yet it produces without possessing, acts without relying and leads without controlling; this is mysterious virtue.

beats.scene: A child holds her mother's hand on a hillside path
beats.summary: Chapter 52: the world had a beginning, which may be called its mother; to know the mother is to know the child, and holding to the mother keeps one safe all through life.

beats.scene: A man sits quietly in his house with the shutters closed
beats.summary: Chapter 52: block the openings and close the doors and there will be no trouble all one's life; seeing the small is clarity and keeping to the soft is strength.

beats.scene: A smooth broad road runs beside a rough, crooked side path
beats.summary: Chapter 53: if the writer had even a little knowledge, he would walk the great Way and fear only to stray from it; the great Way is smooth, but people love the side paths.

beats.scene: A gleaming palace stands beside weedy fields and an empty granary
beats.summary: Chapter 53: when palaces are spotless while the fields are full of weeds and the granaries are empty, and rulers wear fine clothes and carry sharp swords, that is robbers' splendour and not the Tao.

beats.scene: A deep-rooted old tree stands firm in a strong wind
beats.summary: Chapter 54: what is well planted cannot be pulled up, and what is well held cannot slip away, so that children and grandchildren will honour their ancestors for ever.

beats.scene: A single lamp lights a room, then a house, then a whole street
beats.summary: Chapter 54: cultivate virtue in yourself and it becomes real; in the family and it grows; in the village and it lasts; in the country and it flourishes; in the world and it spreads everywhere.

beats.scene: A traveller looks from a hilltop across a village, fields and a far country
beats.summary: Chapter 54: so one should judge a person by the person, a family by the family, a village by the village, a country by the country and the world by the world; this is how the writer knows the world.

beats.scene: A baby sleeps peacefully on a meadow while a butterfly lands near it
beats.summary: Chapter 55: one who is rich in virtue is like a newborn child, whom stinging insects, wild beasts and birds of prey do not harm.

beats.scene: A baby grips a finger tightly and laughs in its mother's arms
beats.summary: Chapter 55: the newborn has soft bones and weak muscles, yet its grip is firm; it can cry all day without becoming hoarse, which shows perfect harmony.

beats.scene: A man puffs out his chest and strains while a baby simply breathes
beats.summary: Chapter 55: to know harmony is to know the constant; to force life is ominous, and to make the mind control the breath is strain; what grows strong then ages is not the Tao.

beats.scene: A sage sits silent among the chatter of a busy market
beats.summary: Chapter 56: those who know do not speak, and those who speak do not know.

beats.scene: A smooth round pebble lies among ordinary dust on a path
beats.summary: Chapter 56: block the openings, blunt what is sharp, untie what is tangled, soften the glare and merge with the dust: this is mysterious sameness, and one who has it cannot be favoured or harmed, honoured or disgraced.

beats.scene: A calm village market with no guards in sight
beats.summary: Chapter 57: rule a country with straightness, fight a war with surprise, and win the world by not meddling.

beats.scene: A town wall covered with notices of rules and fines
beats.summary: Chapter 57: the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people become; the more sharp weapons, the more confusion; the more cleverness, the more strange things; and the more laws, the more thieves.

beats.scene: People work happily in a field while a ruler rests by his gate
beats.summary: Chapter 57: the sage says that if he does nothing the people change themselves, if he loves stillness they become upright, if he does not meddle they prosper, and if he has no desires they become simple.

beats.scene: A stern official with a notebook peers at a nervous crowd
beats.summary: Chapter 58: when government is dull and quiet, the people are simple and honest; when it is sharp and prying, the people become crafty.

beats.scene: A coin balanced upright between two cupped hands
beats.summary: Chapter 58: misfortune is what fortune leans on, and fortune is where misfortune hides; who knows how things will end?

beats.scene: A square stone with softly rounded edges sits in a garden
beats.summary: Chapter 58: the sage is square but does not cut, sharp but does not pierce, straight but not rigid and bright but not dazzling.

beats.scene: A farmer stores grain in a granary before the winter
beats.summary: Chapter 59: in governing people and serving heaven, nothing is like frugality; frugality means early preparation, which means building up virtue, and then nothing is beyond reach.

beats.scene: A thick root spreads beneath a mountain and holds the whole hillside
beats.summary: Chapter 59: when nothing is beyond reach, one's limit is unknown, and one who has the mother of the country can last long; this is deep roots and a firm base, and the way to long life.

beats.scene: A cook gently turns a small fish in a pan
beats.summary: Chapter 60: ruling a large country is like cooking a small fish; too much handling spoils it.

beats.scene: A quiet dark village at night under a calm full moon
beats.summary: Chapter 60: when the world is ruled by the Tao, spirits have no power to harm; not that they lack power, but their power does not hurt people, and neither does the sage.

beats.scene: Many streams run downhill and gather in a wide low river valley
beats.summary: Chapter 61: a great country should be like low ground, the place downstream where all the streams meet, the female of the world.

beats.scene: Two villages, one big and one small, greet each other politely
beats.summary: Chapter 61: a big country that lowers itself before a small one will win the small one, and a small country that lowers itself before a big one will win the big one.

beats.scene: A big town and a little town share one long table at a feast
beats.summary: Chapter 61: the big country wants to unite and care for others and the small one wants to join and serve; each gets what it wants, but the big one should lower itself.

beats.scene: An old lantern glows in a hidden shelter beneath a hill
beats.summary: Chapter 62: the Tao is the hidden shelter of the ten thousand things, the treasure of the good and the refuge of the not good; even a person who is not good should not be thrown away.

beats.scene: A newly crowned emperor receives jade discs and a team of four horses
beats.summary: Chapter 62: when an emperor is crowned, it is better to sit and offer this Tao than jade discs and a team of four horses; the ancients prized it because by it the seeker finds and the sinner is forgiven.

beats.scene: A man hands a cup of water to someone who has quarrelled with him
beats.summary: Chapter 63: act without acting, serve without fuss and taste what has no taste; whether the matter is big or small, repay hatred with virtue.

beats.scene: A boy sorts a small pile of stones before building a high wall
beats.summary: Chapter 63: plan the difficult while it is easy and do the great while it is small; the sage never does anything great and so achieves greatness; he treats everything as difficult, and so has no difficulty.

beats.scene: A small crack in a dam is mended with a handful of clay
beats.summary: Chapter 64: what is at rest is easy to hold, what has not yet appeared is easy to plan for, and what is brittle or tiny is easy to break or scatter; act before things happen and set in order before disorder.

beats.scene: A traveller takes a first step on a long road toward distant mountains
beats.summary: Chapter 64: a tree as thick as a man's embrace grows from a tiny sprout, a nine-storey tower begins with a heap of earth, and a journey of a thousand miles starts beneath one's feet.

beats.scene: A climber places careful steps near the summit of a hill
beats.summary: Chapter 64: those who force things spoil them and those who grasp lose them; people often fail near the end of a task, so be as careful at the end as at the beginning; the sage desires not to desire and helps things be natural.

beats.scene: A wise old ruler shows village children how to plant rice
beats.summary: Chapter 65: those who followed the Tao in ancient times kept the people simple and not scheming; people are hard to rule because they are too clever.

beats.scene: A deep river winds through green hills toward a far sea
beats.summary: Chapter 65: to rule with cleverness harms a country and to rule without it is a blessing; knowing this is a pattern, and knowing the pattern is mysterious virtue, deep and far-reaching.

beats.scene: A broad sea receives rivers from a hundred hills
beats.summary: Chapter 66: rivers and seas are the kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at being lower than them.

beats.scene: A leader walks at the back of a line of travellers
beats.summary: Chapter 66: so the sage who wishes to be above people puts himself below them in his words, and the one who wishes to lead puts himself behind.

beats.scene: Cheerful villagers lift a modest man onto their shoulders
beats.summary: Chapter 66: so the sage is above, and the people do not feel burdened; he is in front, and they are not hurt; the world gladly pushes him forward, and since he does not compete, no one can compete with him.

beats.scene: An old teacher holds three small objects in an open hand
beats.summary: Chapter 67: the world says that the writer's Tao is great but unlike anything; the writer says he has three treasures that he holds and keeps, which are compassion, frugality and not putting himself first.

beats.scene: A brave woman shares her last bread with a hungry child
beats.summary: Chapter 67: because he is compassionate he can be brave, because he is frugal he can be generous, and because he does not put himself first he can become a leader.

beats.scene: A calm defender stands firm at a gate under a bright sky
beats.summary: Chapter 67: people today give up compassion for bravery, frugality for generosity and humility for being first, which is death; compassion wins in battle and holds firm in defence, and heaven protects those who show it.

beats.scene: A calm captain sits quietly while his soldiers rest
beats.summary: Chapter 68: a good warrior is not warlike, a good fighter is not angry, a good conqueror does not engage the enemy, and a good employer is humble.

beats.scene: Two workers carry a heavy beam together, one at each end
beats.summary: Chapter 68: this is called the virtue of not competing and of using the strength of others; it matches heaven, the ancient ultimate.

beats.scene: A guest steps back politely to let the host go first
beats.summary: Chapter 69: strategists say that they dare not play the host but would rather be the guest, and dare not advance an inch but would rather retreat a foot.

beats.scene: A soldier marches in step with no weapon in his hands
beats.summary: Chapter 69: this is called marching without marching, rolling up the sleeves without arms, seizing without weapons and confronting without an enemy.

beats.scene: Two armies face each other across a misty plain, one silent and sad
beats.summary: Chapter 69: there is no greater calamity than underestimating the enemy; when two armies meet, the one that grieves wins.

beats.scene: An old man speaks a few plain words to a young listener
beats.summary: Chapter 70: the writer's words are easy to understand and easy to practise, yet no one in the world can understand or practise them.

beats.scene: A young student frowns at a scroll and cannot understand it
beats.summary: Chapter 70: words have an ancestor and deeds have a master; because people do not know this, they do not know the writer.

beats.scene: A plainly dressed old man with a jade stone hidden inside his coat
beats.summary: Chapter 70: those who know the writer are few, and so he is honoured; the sage wears coarse clothes but carries jade in his heart.

beats.scene: A student smiles and shrugs while closing a large heavy book
beats.summary: Chapter 71: to know that you do not know is best; not to know that you do not know is a sickness.

beats.scene: A man sets down a heavy bag by the roadside and sighs with relief
beats.summary: Chapter 71: only by being sick of the sickness can one be free of it; the sage is not sick because he is sick of the sickness.

beats.scene: A wide meadow with open houses and calm villagers going about their day
beats.summary: Chapter 72: when people do not fear power, a greater power arrives; do not narrow their homes or oppress their livelihood, and then they will not be oppressed.

beats.scene: A quiet man looks at himself in a bowl of water and smiles
beats.summary: Chapter 72: the sage knows himself but does not show himself, and loves himself but does not exalt himself; he leaves the one and takes the other.

beats.scene: A rash man leaps toward a cliff edge as a careful man steps back
beats.summary: Chapter 73: one who is brave in daring will meet his end, and one who is brave in not daring will live; of these two, one brings benefit and one brings harm.

beats.scene: A great calm sky above a still plain at dawn
beats.summary: Chapter 73: who knows why heaven dislikes what it dislikes? Even the sage finds it hard to say; the Way of heaven does not strive, yet it wins; it does not speak, yet it answers.

beats.scene: A vast net of fine threads glitters in the morning light
beats.summary: Chapter 73: heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through it.

beats.scene: A stern judge points at a calm crowd who do not flinch
beats.summary: Chapter 74: if people do not fear death, it is no use threatening them with death.

beats.scene: A young man struggles to lift a master carpenter's heavy axe
beats.summary: Chapter 74: there is always a master executioner, and to take his place is like carving in place of a master carpenter; those who do so rarely escape hurting their own hands.

beats.scene: Hungry villagers watch a tax collector load grain onto a cart
beats.summary: Chapter 75: people go hungry because their rulers eat up too much in taxes, and they are hard to rule because their rulers interfere.

beats.scene: A man relaxes beside a river and does not hurry
beats.summary: Chapter 75: people take death lightly because they struggle so hard for life; one who does not strive for life is wiser than one who prizes it.

beats.scene: A green willow bends in the wind beside a snapped dry branch
beats.summary: Chapter 76: a living person is soft and supple, and a dead one is hard and stiff; living plants are tender and dead ones are dry.

beats.scene: A stiff old stick snaps while a springy reed bends
beats.summary: Chapter 76: so the hard and stiff are companions of death, and the soft and weak are companions of life.

beats.scene: A tall tree is felled while a small bush survives beside it
beats.summary: Chapter 76: a strong army does not win and a strong tree is cut down; the strong and big are below, and the soft and weak are above.

beats.scene: An archer lowers a high bow and raises a low one, adjusting it
beats.summary: Chapter 77: the Way of heaven is like drawing a bow, pressing down what is high and lifting what is low.

beats.scene: A rich man's table is piled high while a poor man's table is bare
beats.summary: Chapter 77: heaven reduces excess and makes up what is lacking, but the way of people is the opposite, taking from those who have too little to give to those who have too much; only one who has the Tao can give his surplus to the world.

beats.scene: A waterfall wears the rock face smooth
beats.summary: Chapter 78: nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, yet nothing is better at attacking the hard and strong, and nothing can take its place.

beats.scene: A king stands among villagers to share the blame after a bad harvest
beats.summary: Chapter 78: the weak overcome the strong and the soft overcome the hard, which everyone knows but no one practises; whoever takes on the disgrace of the country is fit to lead it, and true words seem to say the opposite.

beats.scene: A man holds half a split wooden tally and smiles at a debtor
beats.summary: Chapter 79: after a great quarrel is settled some bitterness remains, so the sage keeps his half of the contract without demanding payment; heaven has no favourites but is always with the good.

beats.scene: A small peaceful village of simple houses beside a quiet river
beats.summary: Chapter 80: in a small country with few people, tools that could do the work of ten or a hundred are not used, people take death seriously and do not move far, and boats, carriages, armour and weapons are not shown off.

beats.scene: Two villages face each other across a river as their roosters crow
beats.summary: Chapter 80: the people return to knotted cords instead of writing, enjoy their food, clothes, homes and customs, and live so close to their neighbours that they hear their roosters and dogs, yet grow old without visiting each other.

beats.scene: A plain wooden cup stands beside a painted, ornate cup
beats.summary: Chapter 81: true words are not beautiful and beautiful words are not true; good people do not argue and those who argue are not good; those who know are not learned and those who are learned do not know.

beats.scene: The sage gives away loaves of bread yet his basket stays full
beats.summary: Chapter 81: the sage does not hoard, and the more he does for others the more he has; the Way of heaven benefits and does not harm, and the way of the sage is to act without competing.

beats.scene: Laozi on his ox rides west through a pass as a gatekeeper watches
beats.summary: An old legend says that Laozi wrote the book for a gatekeeper at the western pass and rode away; historians are unsure, but the book remains.

Short needs long, and high needs low, so they depend on each other.

He helps things grow, but he does not say they are his.
If people do not prize gold, nobody has a reason to steal.

The space between earth and sky is empty, yet it never runs out.
The spirit of the valley never dies.
Her gate is the root of the sky and the earth.
The sky and the earth last long because they live for others.
The wise man steps back, and so he finds himself in front.
He wants nothing for himself, and so he gets what he needs.
The best way to live is the way of water.
Water goes to low places that people do not like.
Good people choose their place well and speak what is true.
Fill a bowl too full, and the water will spill.
When your work is done, step back and let it rest.
Can you breathe as softly as a sleeping baby?
Can you clean the dark mirror of your mind?
She feeds her children and does not own them.
A wheel has many spokes, but its centre is empty.
A potter makes a bowl, and the space inside holds food.
A room is useful because it has space inside.
Too many bright colours can tire your eyes.
The wise man wants what he needs, not what shines.
Praise and blame can both make a person afraid.
A person who loves the world can be trusted with it.
You can look, but you cannot see the Way.

If you meet it, it has no front.

To see this is wise, and it brings us peace.

When the work is done, the people say they did it themselves.
When people forget the Way, they begin to talk about duty.
Good children are praised when the family is in trouble.

Its name has not been lost from the earliest times.
A tree that bends in the wind does not break.

Even earth and sky cannot make wild storms last.
A man who stands on his toes cannot stand for long.
Those who show off do not shine for long.
These habits are like scraps of old food on a plate.

The Way follows what is natural, and so should we.
A calm mind is the master of a restless mind.
A ruler who is always in a hurry loses his way.
A good traveller leaves no tracks behind him.
The wise man helps everyone, and he wastes nothing.
A good person can teach one who is not good.
Know what is strong, but keep to what is soft.
The wise man goes back to the block of plain wood.
If you grip the world too hard, you will lose it.

After a battle, the winners should mourn for the dead.
The Way is like plain wood, small but very strong.
Streams run down the hills into the rivers and seas.
To know other people is clever, but to know yourself is wise.
To rule others is strong, but to rule yourself is mighty.
Someone who knows he has enough is a rich man.
The great Way flows everywhere, to the left and the right.
Because it never tries to be great, it is great.
Hold to the Way, and the world will come to you.
Music and good food make travellers stop and stay.
What is going to shrink must first be allowed to grow.
The soft and weak can overcome the hard and strong.
A fish must not leave the deep water.
The Way does nothing, and yet nothing is left undone.
If rulers followed the Way, the people would settle down.
True goodness does not know that it is good.
When the Way is lost, people turn to rules and ritual.
A wise person prefers the fruit to the flower.
Long ago, the sky became clear and the earth became firm.
Without the One, the earth would crack and split.
The high depends on the low, and the great on the small.
The Way always goes back to where it began.
All things come from something, and that comes from nothing.
A great student hears the Way and follows it well.
The bright path can look dark, and the smooth path rough.
The greatest sound is very faint, and the greatest shape has no form.
The Way gave birth to one, then two, then three.
All things carry the dark and hold the light.
Kings once called themselves by humble names.
The softest thing in the world beats the hardest.
Teaching without words is a gift that few can give.
What is worth more, your good name or yourself?
Those who know when they have enough are never ashamed.
The greatest work may look like it has flaws.
Great skill can look clumsy, and great speech can stumble.
Moving helps with cold, and being still helps with heat.
In peaceful times, horses work on the farm.
Wanting more than we need is the greatest mistake.
You can know the world without leaving your house.
The farther you go, the less you may know.
Learning adds something every day, but the Way takes things away.
Do less and less, and nothing is left undone.
A ruler who keeps out of people's lives can rule the world.
The wise man listens, and he takes the people's hearts as his own.
He is kind to the good, and also to those who are not.
People watch him, and he looks after them like children.
Some people live well, and some move toward death.
They hold on to life too tightly, and so they lose it.
A calm man can walk past tigers without fear.
Everything honours the Way, but no one is ordered to do so.
The Way gives life and protects it without owning it.
The world has a mother, and we are her children.
Close the doors, and your life will have less trouble.
The great Way is smooth, but people love side paths.
The palace shines, but the fields have weeds and the stores are empty.
What is planted well cannot be pulled up easily.
Start with yourself, then your family, then the whole world.
We know the world by looking at what is near.
A baby is safe, even among wild creatures.
A baby's bones are soft, but its grip is strong.
To know harmony is wise, but forcing life brings trouble.
Those who know do not talk, and those who talk do not know.
A wise person blends in with the dust of the world.
The best ruler lets people live their own lives.
The more laws there are, the more thieves there are.
If I do nothing, the people take care of themselves.
A quiet ruler has honest people, and a harsh ruler has tricky ones.
Good luck can hide bad luck, and bad luck can hide good.
A good man is firm, but he does not hurt others.
A wise person saves early, before the hard times come.
Deep roots and a firm base make a long life.
Ruling a big country is like cooking a small fish.
When the Way rules, even spirits do no harm.
A great country should be like low ground where rivers meet.
A big country should be humble toward a small one.
Each country gets what it wants, but the big one should bow first.
The Way is a safe place for all things.
A gift of the Way is better than jade and horses.
Be good to the person who has been bad to you.
Do the hard things while they are still easy.
Mend a small crack before it becomes a big one.
A journey of a thousand miles begins with one step.
Be as careful at the end as at the start.
The old masters kept the people simple, not tricky.
Ruling with tricks hurts a country, and ruling honestly helps it.
The sea is king of the rivers because it lies low.
A wise leader walks behind the people he leads.
The people gladly push him forward, because he never competes.
I have three treasures, and I hold them and keep them.
Kind people can be brave, and people who save can give.
Those who are kind in battle will win and stand firm.

A bold man is in danger, but a careful man lives on.
Heaven does not fight, yet it always wins.

The more the wise man gives, the more he has.

B1B2: The Tao Te Ching is a short book of 81 poems from ancient China. It is said to be the work of a wise man called Laozi, although nobody knows for sure who he was.
The very first chapter of the book begins with a famous puzzle about words. The Tao that can be explained in words, it says, is not the Tao that lasts for ever.
The chapter says that what has no name is the beginning of heaven and earth. Once it is given a name, it becomes the mother of all the things in the world.
When you want nothing, says the first chapter, you can see the mystery of the Tao. When you are full of wanting, you see only the edges of things.
When everyone knows what is beautiful, says the second chapter, the idea of ugliness appears too. Long and short, high and low, before and after, each one needs the other to have any meaning.
The sage, says the chapter, does his work without forcing anything. He teaches without long speeches, because he knows that example is a stronger teacher than talk.
The sage lets all things rise and grow, and he does not turn any of them away. He makes things without owning them, and he finishes his work without holding on to it.
If a ruler does not praise the cleverest people, says the third chapter, they will stop competing with each other. If rare treasures are not prized, nobody will be tempted to steal them.
The wise ruler, says the chapter, empties the people's hearts of craving and fills their stomachs. He makes their bones strong and their ambitions weak, and he keeps them simple.
The fourth chapter compares the Tao to a bowl that is empty, yet is never filled up. It softens what is sharp, unties what is knotted, and settles quietly among the dust of the world.
Heaven and earth are not sentimental, says the fifth chapter. They treat the ten thousand things like straw dogs, which are used in a ceremony and then thrown away.
It is empty, yet it never runs out, and the more it moves, the more it gives. Too much talk wears a person out, so it is better to keep to the quiet centre.
The sixth chapter speaks of the valley spirit, which never dies. It is called the mysterious female, because it quietly gives birth to everything.
The gate of the mysterious female is the root of heaven and earth. It seems to go on and on, and however much one uses it, it is never used up.
Heaven and earth are long-lasting, says the seventh chapter. The reason is that they do not live for themselves, and so they are able to live for a very long time.
In the same way, the sage puts himself last, and he finds that he is first. He stays outside the quarrel, and for that reason he stays safe.
Is it not because he wants nothing for himself, the chapter asks, that he is able to fulfil himself? A person with no selfish aim can never be disappointed.
The highest good is like water, says the eighth chapter. Water gives life to all things and does not fight with any of them.
Water settles in the low places that people usually avoid. That is why, the chapter says, it is so close to the Tao.

The good person, says the chapter, lives in the right place and keeps a deep heart. He gives kindly, speaks truly, works well and acts at the right time, and because he does not compete, nobody blames him.
It is better to stop than to fill a bowl to the brim, says the ninth chapter. If you keep sharpening a blade, it will soon become too thin to last.
When a hall is full of gold and jade, no one is able to guard it. A person who is proud of his riches and his rank invites trouble, and the wise way is to withdraw when the work is done.
The tenth chapter asks a series of questions, and the first is about the body and the spirit. Can you keep them together, and can you breathe as gently and softly as a newborn baby?
Can you wash the dark mirror of the mind until it has no stain? Can you love the people and lead them without cleverness?

The chapter ends with a picture of a gentle parent who gives life, makes things without owning them and leads without trying to control. This quiet kind of generosity, says the writer, is what he calls mysterious virtue.
Thirty spokes come together at the hub of a wheel. It is the empty space in the middle, says the eleventh chapter, that makes the wheel useful.
Clay is shaped into a pot, and the potter is proud of the clay. But the hollow space inside the pot is the part that holds water, and that makes it useful.
We cut doors and windows to make a room, and the empty space inside is what we live in. So what exists gives us advantage, while what does not exist gives us use.
The twelfth chapter warns that too many colours can blind the eye. Too many sounds can deafen the ear, and too many rich flavours can spoil the taste.
Racing and hunting make the mind wild, says the chapter, and rare treasures lead people to do wrong. The sage looks after what he truly needs and does not run after what only looks good.
Both favour and disgrace give a person a fright, says the thirteenth chapter. If you are praised, you fear losing the praise, and if you are blamed, you fear what comes next.
We have great troubles, says the chapter, because we are so worried about ourselves. Someone who treats the world as dearly as his own body can be trusted to look after it.
Look at it, says the fourteenth chapter, and you will not see it. Listen for it and you will not hear it, and if you reach out to hold it, you will find nothing in your hand.
Above, it is not bright, and below, it is not dark. It goes on without end, it has no name, and in the end it returns to nothing, like a shape without a shape.
Meet it, and you will not see a front. Follow it, and you will not see a back, but if you hold on to the ancient Way, you can deal with the present.

The masters of old, says the fifteenth chapter, were so subtle and deep that nobody could really understand them. All the writer can do is describe how they seemed, and the first picture is of a man crossing a stream in winter.
They were as polite as guests, and they were yielding like ice that is beginning to melt. They were plain like a block of uncut wood, open like a valley, and cloudy like muddy water.

Muddy water becomes clear if it is left still, says the fifteenth chapter, and it clears itself little by little. Those who follow the Tao do not wish to be full, and because they are never full, they can always begin again.
Reach the greatest emptiness, says the sixteenth chapter, and hold on to stillness. The ten thousand things rise up and flourish, and the writer watches each one return to its root.

Returning to the root is stillness, says the chapter, and to know this is to be wise. Whoever does not know it stumbles into trouble, but whoever knows it is open-minded, fair and at peace, even at the end of life.
The best ruler, says the seventeenth chapter, is one whom the people hardly know is there. The next best is loved and praised, the next is feared, and the worst is despised.
Where there is not enough trust, says the chapter, there will be distrust. A good ruler speaks little, and when his work is finished, the people all say that they did it themselves.
When the great Way is lost, says the eighteenth chapter, people start to talk about kindness and duty. When cleverness appears, there is a great deal of pretending too.
When a family is not at peace, says the chapter, people begin to praise dutiful children. When a country is in chaos, people begin to praise loyal ministers.

Give up cleverness and wise-sounding schemes, says the nineteenth chapter, and people will be a hundred times better off. Give up showy kindness and duty, and they will return to a natural love for each other.

Give up skill and profit, says the chapter, and there will be no thieves. These three things are not enough by themselves, so show what is plain, hold to what is simple, and want only a little for yourself.
Everyone else is enjoying a great feast, as if they were climbing a terrace in spring. I alone sit quietly, says the writer of the twentieth chapter, like a baby who has not yet learned to smile.
The writer feels weary, as though he had no home to go to. Other people have more than they need, and only he seems to have lost everything and to have the mind of a fool.
Ordinary people seem bright and clear, but the writer is dim and dull. He is as calm as the sea and he drifts about, as if there were no place where he had to stop.

Everyone else has a plan and a purpose, but the writer says that he is stubborn and plain, like a country person. He alone is different, because he values being fed by the great Mother, which is the Way.
The twenty-first chapter says that great virtue follows the Tao and nothing else. The Tao is vague and hard to catch, yet inside it there are images, things and something pure at the heart.
This pure essence is real, and it can be trusted. Its name has never disappeared since the earliest times, and through it, says the writer, he can see how all things begin.
The twenty-second chapter gives a list of surprising truths. What bends will become whole, what is crooked will become straight, and what is hollow will be filled.
The sage holds to the One, and he becomes an example for the whole world. Because he does not show himself off, he shines, and because he does not argue that he is right, people respect him.
He does not boast, so his work is valued, and he does not brag, so his name lasts. Since he does not compete with anyone, no one in the world can compete with him.
To speak little is natural, says the twenty-third chapter. A whirlwind does not blow for a whole morning, and a heavy rainstorm does not last for a whole day.
Heaven and earth make the storm, and even they cannot make it last, so how much less can a person? Those who follow the Tao become one with the Tao, and those who lack trust will not be trusted.
One who stands on tiptoe cannot stand firmly, says the twenty-fourth chapter. One who takes huge strides cannot walk very far, because he soon grows tired.
Those who put themselves on show do not shine, says the chapter, and those who always say they are right are not respected. Boasting earns no real merit, and bragging does not last.
In the light of the Tao, says the chapter, these habits are like leftover food and useless baggage. Everyone dislikes them, and so a person who follows the Tao does not stay in them.

The twenty-fifth chapter describes something whole and silent that existed before heaven and earth. It stands alone, it never changes, and it moves everywhere without growing tired, so it may be the mother of the world.
The writer admits that he does not know its name, so he calls it the Tao. If he must describe it, he says, he would call it great, because to be great is to go far and then to return.
The Tao is great, heaven is great, earth is great, and the king is great too. People follow the earth, the earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Tao, and the Tao follows what is natural.

The heavy is the root of the light, says the twenty-sixth chapter, and stillness is the master of restlessness. For this reason a wise traveller does not leave his baggage wagon behind, even on a long day's journey.
Although the sage may see splendid sights, he stays calm and he is not carried away by them. How can the lord of a great kingdom behave in a light and foolish way?

A good traveller leaves no tracks, says the twenty-seventh chapter, and a good speaker makes no mistakes. A good door needs no bolt and yet cannot be opened, and a good knot needs no rope and yet cannot be untied.
In the same way, the sage is good at helping people, so nobody is thrown away. He is also good at saving things, so nothing is wasted, and this is called following the light.
The good person, says the chapter, is the teacher of the person who is not good. The one who is not good is the material the good person works with, and whoever forgets this will be greatly confused.
Know what it is to be strong, says the twenty-eighth chapter, but keep to what is gentle. Then you will be like a valley that the whole world flows into, and you will return to the state of a child.

Know glory, says the chapter, but keep to humility, and return to the uncarved block of wood. When the block is cut, it becomes tools, and the sage uses them to lead, yet the best carving cuts very little.

Those who want to take the world and improve it by force, says the twenty-ninth chapter, will not succeed. The world is a sacred vessel that cannot be forced, so those who act on it spoil it, and those who grasp it lose it.
Some people lead and some follow, some are strong and some are weak, some rise and some fall. The sage, therefore, avoids what is extreme, what is excessive and what is extravagant.

A ruler who follows the Tao does not force the world with weapons, because force always comes back on the one who uses it. Where armies have camped, says the thirtieth chapter, thorns grow, and a great war is followed by bad years.
A good commander achieves what he came to do and then he stops. He does not boast about it or brag, and he does not take pride in it, because he acted only when he had no choice.
When things reach their full strength, says the chapter, they begin to age. This is not the way of the Tao, and whatever goes against the Tao will soon come to an end.
Weapons, says the thirty-first chapter, are tools of bad luck, and people do not like them. A person who follows the Tao does not make a home among them.
Weapons are not the tools of a gentleman, says the chapter, and he uses them only when he has no other choice. Calm and quiet restraint is the best course, and a victory is nothing to admire.
When many people have been killed, says the chapter, they should be mourned with deep sorrow. Even a victory, it adds, should be marked with the rites of a funeral.

The Tao is always nameless, says the thirty-second chapter, like a block of uncarved wood. Although it seems small, nothing in the world can master it, and if kings could hold to it, all things would come to them freely.
Once the block is cut, there are names, and it is wise to know when to stop. The Tao in the world, says the chapter, is like a stream that runs down into a great river and then into the sea.
Whoever knows other people is clever, says the thirty-third chapter, but whoever knows himself is truly wise. It is much easier to study the faults of others than to look honestly at our own.
To master other people takes force, says the chapter, but to master oneself takes real strength. A man who has beaten every rival may still be a slave to his own temper.
The one who knows contentment is rich, says the chapter, and the one who keeps to his place will last. A person who dies but is not forgotten, it adds, has lived a very long life.
The great Tao flows everywhere, to the left and to the right. All things depend on it for life, and it does not turn any of them away, yet it does not claim any credit.
Because the Tao is always without desire, it may be called small. Because all things return to it and it does not rule them, it may be called great.
Hold fast to the great image, says the thirty-fifth chapter, and the whole world will come to you. They will come without being harmed, and they will find safety, peace and calm.
Music and good food will make passing guests stop, but the Tao seems bland when it is spoken of. You cannot see it or hear it, yet you can never use it all up.
If you want to shrink something, says the thirty-sixth chapter, first let it grow. If you want to weaken something, first let it be strong, and if you want to take, first give.
The soft and the weak overcome the hard and the strong, says the chapter. This is the quiet principle that lies behind all the sayings before it.
A fish should not be taken out of the deep water, says the chapter, and a state should not show off its sharpest weapons. Strength that is hidden is safer than strength that is displayed.
The thirty-seventh chapter is the last of the first half of the book, and it holds a famous paradox. The Tao always does nothing, it says, and yet nothing is left undone.

If kings could hold on to it, the chapter says, all things would change of their own accord. If desire arose, the plain, nameless block of wood would calm it, and the whole world would settle by itself.

The thirty-eighth chapter opens the second half of the book with a paradox about virtue. High virtue never thinks of itself as virtue, so it is real; low virtue never forgets its goodness, so it has none.

When the Way is lost, says the chapter, there is virtue, and when virtue is lost, there is kindness. After kindness comes duty, and after duty comes ritual, which the writer calls the thin edge of loyalty and the beginning of disorder.
Foreknowledge, says the chapter, is the flower of the Tao and the beginning of folly. The great person therefore lives in what is thick, not what is thin, and in the fruit, not the flower.
In ancient times, says the thirty-ninth chapter, certain things attained the One. Heaven became clear, the earth became steady, the spirits became powerful, and the valleys became full.
Without clarity, says the chapter, heaven would crack, and without steadiness, the earth would split. Without power the spirits would fade, and without water the valleys would dry up.

The noble have the humble as their root, says the chapter, and the high have the low as their base. That is why kings call themselves lonely and unworthy, and why a carriage that has been taken apart is no longer a carriage.
Returning is the movement of the Tao, says the fortieth chapter, and yielding is the way in which it works. It is one of the shortest chapters in the whole book.
The ten thousand things of the world are born from what can be seen, the chapter says. What can be seen is born in its turn from what cannot be seen, which the writer calls non-being.
The best student, says the forty-first chapter, hears the Tao and follows it with great effort. The middling student keeps it and then loses it, and the lowest student laughs out loud.
A list of very old sayings follows, and each one turns an expectation upside down. The bright Tao seems dark, the Tao that moves forward seems to be going back, and the smooth Tao seems rough.

The great square has no corners, says the chapter, and the great vessel is slow to finish, while the great sound is faint. The Tao is hidden and has no name, yet it alone feeds and completes all things.
The Tao gave birth to one, says the forty-second chapter, and one gave birth to two. Two gave birth to three, and three gave birth to the ten thousand things.
All things carry yin on their backs, says the chapter, and they hold yang in their arms. By blending these two kinds of energy, they find harmony.
People hate to be called lonely, orphaned or unworthy, says the chapter, yet kings and lords use these very names for themselves. Things may gain by losing, and they may lose by gaining.
The softest thing in the world, says the forty-third chapter, can ride over the hardest. What has no substance at all can enter even a place where there is no space.
Teaching without words, says the chapter, and doing without forcing are of great value. Few people in the world can reach them, though they are available to anyone.
Which is dearer to you, the chapter asks, your good name or your own self? Which matters more, yourself or your wealth, and which is worse, to gain or to lose?

Great love, says the chapter, brings great cost, and hoarding a great deal means losing a great deal. If you know when you have enough, you will not be disgraced, and if you know when to stop, you will not be in danger.
Great perfection seems to have a flaw, says the forty-fifth chapter, yet its use never wears out. Great fullness seems to be empty, yet it never runs dry.
What is truly straight may seem bent, says the chapter, and great skill may seem clumsy. Great speech may seem to stumble, because the best speaker does not need to impress anyone.
Movement overcomes the cold, says the chapter, and stillness overcomes the heat. A mind that is clear and calm can serve as the standard for the whole world.
When the Tao is present in the world, says the forty-sixth chapter, fast horses are used to carry manure for the fields. When it is absent, war horses are bred on the borders of the country.
There is no greater trouble, says the chapter, than not knowing when you have enough. There is no greater fault than wanting more, and whoever knows that enough is enough will always have enough.
Without going out of the door, says the forty-seventh chapter, you can know the whole world. Without looking out of the window, you can see the Way of heaven.
The farther a person goes, the less he may know, says the chapter. The sage knows without travelling, he names things without seeing them, and he gets things done without acting.
In the pursuit of learning, says the forty-eighth chapter, something is added every day. In the pursuit of the Tao, something is dropped every day.
Less and less is done, says the chapter, until at last one reaches doing nothing. When nothing is forced, nothing is left undone, just as a garden grows while the gardener sleeps.
The world is always won by not meddling, says the chapter. Whoever starts to meddle in everything is not fit to rule it.
The sage has no fixed mind of his own, says the forty-ninth chapter. He takes the minds of the people as his own, and so he listens before he decides.
I am good to the good, says the sage, and I am good to the not good, for that is virtue. I trust the trustworthy, and I trust the untrustworthy too, and in this way trust is created.
The sage lives in the world with great care, and he blends his mind with the minds of others. The people all fix their eyes and ears on him, and he treats them as his own children.

The fiftieth chapter says that going out is life and coming back in is death. Of every ten people, some follow life, some follow death, and some, though they are alive, are moving toward death by their own actions.
The writer says this happens because people hold on to life too tightly, as if they could stop it slipping away. They are so busy protecting life that they forget to live it.

The writer has heard that one who knows how to live well can walk through the hills without meeting a tiger. In the same way, such a person goes through a battle without harm, because there is no place in him for death to enter.

The Tao gives birth to things, says the fifty-first chapter, and virtue feeds them. The ten thousand things honour the Tao and value virtue, not because anyone commands them to, but because it is natural.

The Tao gives birth to things and feeds them, makes them grow, and shelters and protects them. It makes without owning, acts without leaning on its own work, and leads without controlling, which is called mysterious virtue.

The world had a beginning, says the fifty-second chapter, and that beginning may be called its mother. If you know the mother, you can know her children, and if you hold on to the mother, you will be safe all your life.
Block the openings, says the chapter, and close the doors, and you will have no trouble all your life. To see what is small is clarity, and to keep to what is soft is strength.
If I had even a little knowledge, says the writer, I would walk the great Way and fear only to wander from it. The great Way is smooth and easy, and yet people love the side paths.

The palace is spotless, says the chapter, while the fields are full of weeds and the storehouses are empty. The rulers wear fine clothes and carry sharp swords, and that, says the writer, is the splendour of robbers, not the Way.

What is well planted cannot be pulled up, says the fifty-fourth chapter, and what is well held cannot slip away. Because of this, the children and grandchildren will honour their ancestors for generations.
Cultivate virtue in yourself, says the chapter, and it will become real. Cultivate it in the family, and it will grow, and in the village, and it will last, and in the country, and it will flourish.
