So look at a person by the person, says the chapter, and a family by the family. Look at a village by the village, a country by the country, and the world by the world.
One who is rich in virtue, says the fifty-fifth chapter, is like a newborn child. Stinging insects do not sting such a child, wild beasts do not seize it, and birds of prey do not strike.
The bones of a newborn are soft and its muscles are weak, says the chapter, and yet its grip is firm. It can cry all day without becoming hoarse, which is a sign of perfect harmony.
To know harmony is to know what lasts, says the chapter, and to know what lasts is to be wise. Forcing life is a bad sign, and what grows strong only to grow old is not the Tao.
Those who know do not speak, says the fifty-sixth chapter, and those who speak do not know. It is a neat saying, although a clever reader may smile that the writer used so many words to say it.

Block the openings, says the chapter, blunt what is sharp, untie what is tangled, soften the glare and settle in the dust. A person who does this cannot be favoured or harmed, honoured or disgraced, and so the world treasures him.
Rule a country with honesty, says the fifty-seventh chapter, and fight a war with surprise. But the world is won only by those who do not meddle in people's lives.

The more prohibitions there are, says the chapter, the poorer the people become. The more cleverness there is, the more strange things appear, and the more laws there are, the more thieves there will be.
Therefore the sage says, I do nothing, and the people change themselves. I love stillness, and the people become upright, and I want nothing, and the people become simple.
When the government is quiet and dull, says the fifty-eighth chapter, the people are simple and honest. When the government is sharp and prying, the people become crafty.
Misfortune is what good fortune leans on, says the chapter, and fortune is where misfortune hides. Nobody can say how things will end, because there is no fixed standard.
The sage is square, says the chapter, but he does not cut others with his corners. He is straight but not stiff, and he is bright but not dazzling.

In governing people and in serving heaven, says the fifty-ninth chapter, there is nothing like frugality. Frugality means preparing early, preparing early means building up virtue, and then nothing is beyond your reach.

When nothing is beyond your reach, nobody knows your limit, and then you can look after a whole country. One who has the mother of the country will last long, which is called deep roots and a firm base.
Ruling a large country, says the sixtieth chapter, is like cooking a small fish. If you handle it too much, it will fall to pieces.

When the world is ruled by the Tao, says the chapter, the spirits do not harm anyone. It is not that they lack power, but that their power does not hurt people, and the sage does not hurt them either.

A great country, says the sixty-first chapter, should be like low ground, the place downstream where all the streams of the world meet. In the writer's language, it is the female of the world, because it wins by lying low.
A big country that lowers itself before a small one, says the chapter, will win the small one's trust. A small country that lowers itself before a big one will win the big one's protection.

The big country wants to bring people together and look after them, says the chapter, and the small country wants to join and to serve. Each can get what it wants, but the big country should be the one to lower itself.
The Tao is the hidden shelter of the ten thousand things, says the sixty-second chapter. It is the treasure of the good person and the refuge of the person who is not good.
When an emperor is crowned, says the chapter, people bring him jade discs and teams of four horses. It would be better, the writer thinks, to sit quietly and offer him this Tao.
Act without acting, says the sixty-third chapter, work without fuss, and taste what has no taste. Whether a matter is big or small, many or few, answer hatred with virtue.
Plan for the difficult while it is easy, says the chapter, and do the great while it is small. The sage never tries to do anything great, and that is how he achieves it.
What is quiet is easy to hold, says the sixty-fourth chapter, and what has not yet appeared is easy to plan for. What is brittle is easy to break, so act before the trouble comes.
A tree as thick as a man's embrace grows from a tiny sprout. A tower nine storeys high begins as a heap of earth, and a journey of a thousand miles begins beneath your feet.
Those who force things spoil them, says the chapter, and those who grasp lose what they hold. People often fail when they are almost done, so be as careful at the end as at the beginning.

The people who followed the Tao in ancient times, says the sixty-fifth chapter, did not make others clever. They kept the people simple, because people are hard to govern when they are too full of schemes.

To rule a country with cleverness harms the country, says the chapter, and to rule it without cleverness is a blessing. To know these two things is to have a model, and to keep the model in mind is called mysterious virtue.
Rivers and seas are the kings of the hundred valleys, says the sixty-sixth chapter. They are kings because they are good at lying below them, and so all the streams flow to them.
The sage, therefore, who wishes to be above the people puts himself below them when he speaks. If he wishes to lead them, he places himself behind them.

So the sage is above the people, yet they do not feel his weight, and he is in front, yet they are not hurt. The whole world is happy to push him forward and never grows tired of it, because he does not compete.

Everyone says that my Tao is great but that it is not like anything else, says the sixty-seventh chapter. I have three treasures, the writer adds, that I hold and keep, and they are compassion, frugality and not putting myself first.
Because I am compassionate, says the writer, I can be brave, and because I am frugal, I can be generous. Because I do not dare to put myself first, I am able to become a leader.
People today give up compassion and try to be brave, says the chapter, and they give up frugality and try to be generous. They give up humility and try to be first, and this leads to death.

A good warrior is not warlike, says the sixty-eighth chapter, and a good fighter does not lose his temper. A good conqueror does not seek the enemy out, and a good leader of workers speaks to them humbly.
This, says the chapter, is called the virtue of not competing, and it means using the strength of other people. It matches the way of heaven, which is the highest and oldest way of all.
There is a saying among soldiers, says the sixty-ninth chapter, that it is better to be the guest than the host. It is also better to retreat a foot than to advance an inch.
This, says the chapter, is called marching without marching and rolling up the sleeves without having any arms to show. It means seizing without weapons and facing an enemy without one.
There is no greater disaster, says the chapter, than underestimating the enemy, for that nearly costs me my treasure. When two armies meet on equal terms, the one that grieves is the one that wins.
My words are very easy to understand, says the seventieth chapter, and they are very easy to put into practice. Yet nobody in the world seems able to understand them or practise them.
My words have an ancestor, says the writer, and my deeds have a master. It is because people do not know this that they do not know me.
Those who know me are few, says the writer, and that is why I am honoured. The sage wears coarse clothes, but inside his coat he carries a precious piece of jade.
To know that you do not know is the best thing, says the seventy-first chapter. Not to know that you do not know is a kind of sickness.
Only if you are tired of the sickness, says the chapter, can you be free of it. The sage is not sick, because he is tired of being sick in this way.
When people no longer fear the ruler's power, says the seventy-second chapter, something far greater will come. So do not make their homes narrow, and do not make their living hard.
So the sage knows himself, says the chapter, but he does not put himself on show. He loves himself, but he does not think himself above others, and so he leaves the one and takes the other.
A man who is brave in daring, says the seventy-third chapter, will meet his end. A man who is brave in not daring will live, and of these two, one brings benefit and the other brings harm.
Who can say why heaven dislikes what it dislikes? Even the sage finds it hard to say, but the Way of heaven does not strive, and yet it is good at winning.
Heaven's net is vast, says the chapter, and although its mesh is wide, nothing slips through it. The great pattern of things is patient, but it misses nothing.
If people do not fear death, says the seventy-fourth chapter, there is no point in frightening them with death. A ruler who has only threats left has very little left to rule with.
There is always a master executioner, says the chapter, and to take his place is like carving in place of a master carpenter. Those who try it seldom escape without hurting their own hands.
People are hungry, says the seventy-fifth chapter, because their rulers eat up too much in taxes. They are hard to rule, too, because their rulers interfere with them.
People take death lightly, says the chapter, because they struggle so hard to hold on to life. Someone who is not anxious about life is wiser than someone who prizes it too much.
When a person is alive, says the seventy-sixth chapter, his body is soft and supple, and when he is dead, it is hard and stiff. Living plants are soft and tender, and dead ones are dry and brittle.
So what is hard and stiff is a companion of death, says the chapter, and what is soft and weak is a companion of life. In other words, the gentle things are the ones that go on living and growing.
An army that is too strong does not win, says the chapter, and a tree that is too strong gets cut down. The strong and the big lose their place, while the soft and the weak take it.
The Way of heaven is like the drawing of a bow, says the seventy-seventh chapter. The high part is pressed down and the low part is raised up.
Heaven's Way reduces what is too much and makes up what is too little. The way of people is the opposite, since it takes from those who have too little and gives to those who already have too much.
Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, says the seventy-eighth chapter. Yet when it attacks the hard and strong, nothing can do better, and nothing can take its place.
The weak overcome the strong and the soft overcome the hard, says the chapter. Everyone knows this, yet almost no one practises it, and true words often seem to say the opposite of what we expect.

After a great quarrel has been settled, says the seventy-ninth chapter, some bitterness always remains. So the sage keeps his half of the contract, and he does not demand payment from the one who owes him.
Let a country be small and its people few, says the eightieth chapter. They do not use tools that could do the work of a hundred men, and they have no wish to travel far.

Let people go back to keeping records with knotted cords, says the chapter, and let them enjoy their food, their clothes and their homes. A neighbouring village is so near that they hear its roosters and dogs, yet they grow old without ever visiting it.
True words are not beautiful, says the eighty-first chapter, and beautiful words are not true. Good people do not argue, and people who argue are not good.
The sage does not hoard, says the last chapter. The more he does for others, the more he has himself, and the more he gives, the more he gains.

An old story says that Laozi wrote these words for a gatekeeper at a mountain pass and then rode away on his ox. Nobody knows whether the story is true, but the little book has been read and translated for centuries.
C1C2: The Tao Te Ching is a small book from ancient China, made of eighty-one short chapters, and its title is often translated as the Way and its Power. Tradition gives it to a sage called Laozi, whose name means Old Master, although no historian can say for certain who he was or when he lived. Its words are few and its pictures are simple, yet people have gone on reading it, in every century, for more than two thousand years.

The very first chapter opens with a riddle that sets the tone for the whole book. The Way that can be told in words, it says, is not the lasting Way, and the name that can be spoken is not the lasting name. Anyone who wishes to understand the Tao must therefore be ready to hold a little silence beside every sentence.

What has no name, says the chapter, was there at the beginning of heaven and earth, before anything had been called anything at all. Once a name is given, it becomes the mother of the ten thousand things, which is the old way of saying everything that lives and grows. The nameless and the named are not two different things, but one thing seen from two sides.

Someone who is free from desire, the chapter explains, is able to see the hidden depth of the Way, while someone full of wanting sees only its outer shape. The two ways of looking come from the same source and differ only in their names, so that the darkness inside darkness turns out to be a gate. Through that one gate, the author says, every wonder in the whole world finds its way into being.

The second chapter observes that once people agree on what is beautiful, they have also made something ugly, and once they agree on what is good, they have made something bad. Being and not being give birth to each other, the difficult and the easy complete each other, and the long and the short measure each other. Nothing in the world stands alone, and the sage learns to see each thing together with its partner.

Following this view, the sage goes about his work without pushing, and he teaches without a single speech. He does not tell people what to think; he simply lives so that they can see how a calm person acts. In this way the lesson enters quietly, like water into dry ground, and nobody feels that they have been lectured.

When the ten thousand things appear, the sage neither commands them nor sends them away, but lets each one rise in its own season. He creates without claiming, he works without expecting reward, and when the task is complete he does not stay to be admired. Because he does not cling to what he has done, the chapter concludes, his work never leaves him.

In the third chapter the author turns to the ruler and offers him some quiet but surprising advice. If he does not put the most talented on a pedestal, his people will not quarrel over who is best, and if he does not prize rare treasures, they will not be tempted to become thieves. A heart that is never shown what to crave, he suggests, will stay calm and quite content with its lot.

A good ruler, the chapter says, empties the heart of restless craving and fills the belly, softens ambition and strengthens the bones. Those who are simple in their wants have little to scheme about, and those who do scheme find that nobody is listening. When one acts without forcing, the author promises, nothing at all is left in disorder.

The Way, says the fourth chapter, is like a deep bowl that can be poured into all day without ever being full. It blunts the sharp edge, loosens the knot, softens the glare and settles down among the ordinary dust of the world. The writer admits that he does not know whose child it is, and thinks it may be older than any ruler or god.

Heaven and earth are not sentimental, says the fifth chapter, and they treat the ten thousand things as people once treated straw dogs, which were honoured during a ceremony and then cast aside. The rain falls on the good and the bad field alike, and the sun does not ask who deserves it. The sage, in the same way, is fair to all and plays no favourites among his people.

The space between heaven and earth, the chapter says, is like a blacksmith's bellows, which is hollow inside and yet never runs dry. The more it is worked, the more breath comes out of it, and what looks like nothing turns out to be a source of endless power. Many words, by contrast, only tire the speaker, so the wise person chooses to hold fast to the still centre.

In the sixth chapter the writer turns to the spirit of the valley, an empty place where streams gather and green things grow. This spirit never dies, and he calls it the mysterious female, since it quietly brings forth all that lives. It does not push or shout or ask for thanks, yet nothing comes into being without its help.

The gate of the mysterious female, the chapter continues, is the root from which heaven and earth themselves grew. It is thin as a thread that never breaks, and it seems always to be there, hardly noticed, like a spring in the hills. Use it as much as you like, says the author, and it will never be used up.

Heaven and earth endure, the seventh chapter tells us, because they do not exist for their own sake. The sun does not shine in order to be thanked, and the earth does not bear fruit in order to be praised. Because they ask for nothing in return, nothing in the world is able to wear them out.

The sage follows the example of the heavens, putting himself last, and the strange result is that he ends up in the front. He stays outside the struggle for honour and reputation, and so the struggle never really touches him. It is a paradox that the whole book enjoys, since it shows that those who do not push are often the ones who are carried forward.

Is it not precisely because the sage is without selfish aims, asks the chapter, that his own needs are in the end completely met? A man who grabs at everything lives in dread of losing it, while a man who grabs at nothing sleeps well. The sage's quiet reward is that, having asked for nothing at all, he is never left with nothing.

The eighth chapter gives us one of the most famous images in the whole book: the highest good is like water. Water brings life to the ten thousand things and never competes with any of them, flowing around a stone rather than quarrelling with it. It is soft and yielding, and yet nothing in the world can stop it.

Water is content to settle in the low and muddy places that most people hurry to avoid. By taking the humble position, it comes to rest in the very place where everything finally arrives. That is why the writer says that water is almost the same as the Way itself.

In a long list, the eighth chapter describes the person who lives like water: he chooses his home wisely, keeps a heart as deep as a pool, gives with kindness, speaks with honesty and governs with order. He works with skill, and he acts at exactly the right moment, neither too early nor too late. Since he is not fighting anyone, there is no one left to blame him.

Hold a bowl that is filled to the brim, says the ninth chapter, and you will find that it spills with the slightest movement; it would have been wiser to stop pouring earlier. A blade that is sharpened again and again becomes so thin that it cannot be kept for long. The lesson is that every good thing has its limit, and that pushing past it turns the good into harm.

When a hall is crowded with gold and jade, nobody can guard it forever, and the person who grows arrogant on the strength of wealth and rank is preparing his own downfall. The ninth chapter says that the way of heaven is quite different, for heaven finishes its work and quietly steps back. The seasons turn in just this manner, and the sage is advised to follow them.

The tenth chapter does not give orders; it asks questions, and the first one is about wholeness. Can you keep the body and the spirit together without letting them drift apart, and can you make your breath as soft and gentle as a baby's? The writer seems to say that the answer lies not in effort but in a kind of easy attention.

Can you wipe the dark mirror of the mind until not a single spot remains on it, asks the writer, so that it shows things exactly as they are? Can you love the people and govern the country without resorting to clever tricks? Each of these questions points the same way, toward a mind that is clear, honest and quiet.

The tenth chapter ends by describing the Way at work, which is rather like a good parent. It gives life and feeds it, makes without owning, acts without expecting any thanks, and leads without trying to control the ones it leads. This quiet generosity is what the book means by mysterious virtue, the power that does not announce itself.

Thirty spokes share the hub of one cartwheel, says the eleventh chapter, but it is the empty space in the middle of the hub that lets the wheel turn on its axle. Wood and iron are the parts we see and admire, yet without the hole at the centre they would be useless. The first lesson is that what is missing may matter as much as what is there.

A potter takes soft clay and shapes it into a vessel, and everyone praises the beauty of the clay and the skill of the hands. Yet the vessel is useful only because of the hollow space inside it, which holds the water, the grain or the wine. Take away the emptiness, and the finest pot in the world is only a lump.

People cut doors and windows into the walls to make a room, and what they really use is the empty space between the walls. The walls give us shelter, but the emptiness gives us somewhere to live, to sleep and to gather. So what is there offers us advantage, says the chapter, while what is not there offers us use.

Too many colours, the twelfth chapter warns, can leave the eye unable to see, and too many sounds can leave the ear unable to hear. Even rich flavours, if they come in endless variety and are never left alone, will in the end spoil the tongue. Anyone who has stood in a crowded fairground, dazzled and deafened, will know what the old writer meant.

Racing horses and hunting wild animals can make the mind restless and wild, and rare goods tempt people to act badly in order to get them. The sage therefore looks after the belly and not the eye, caring for what really nourishes him and not for what merely dazzles. He leaves the showy thing alone, and he takes instead what is plain, honest and quite enough for a good life.

The thirteenth chapter says that favour and disgrace are equally alarming, since both make a person tremble. When you receive praise, you at once begin to fear that you might lose it, and when you lose it, you feel the shame of having once held it. Whoever lives by the opinion of other people is therefore never truly at peace, for the weather of praise keeps changing.

We suffer so much, says the chapter, because we are so attached to ourselves, since without the self there would be little left to worry about. The one who values the world as dearly as his own body, who loves it as he loves himself, is the one to whom the world can safely be given. The rule of a gentle person, in other words, begins with a wide heart.

Look for the Way, says the fourteenth chapter, and you will not see it, so we call it formless; listen for it and you will not hear it, so we call it soundless. Reach out to hold it and your fingers will close on nothing, so we call it untouchable. These three, the chapter adds, cannot be pulled apart and questioned, because at bottom they are only one.

Above, the Way is not bright, and below, it is not dark, but it stretches on without a break and cannot be given a name. In the end it goes back to nothingness, like a form that has no form or an image that has no image. The writer calls it vague and elusive, and he does not pretend that he can make it any clearer.

Come to meet it, says the chapter, and you will not see its face; follow behind it, and you will not see its back. Yet if a person holds on to the ancient Way, he can manage the things of the present day, and if he knows the ancient beginning, he has found the thread of the Tao. It is a thin thread, but it leads through the whole labyrinth of life.

The masters of the old days, says the fifteenth chapter, were so subtle and so deep that ordinary people could not fully understand them. Since description is all that is possible, the writer paints a picture: they were careful as a man who crosses a frozen stream in winter, and watchful as a man who senses that danger lies on every side. Their care was not fear but a respect for the ground beneath their feet.

They were courteous, like guests in another person's house, and they gave way easily, like ice that has begun to melt in the spring. They were plain as a block of wood that has not been carved, as open as an empty valley, and as cloudy as a pool that has been stirred. None of these pictures is flattering, which is exactly what makes them so convincing.

Who can make muddy water clear, asks the chapter, and the answer is that nobody needs to, because water left perfectly still will clear itself in time. In the same way, a still mind that is gently stirred into action will find the right moves slowly, without any hurry. Those who hold to the Way do not want to be filled to the brim, and it is for that very reason that they can be renewed again and again.

Reach the very limit of emptiness, says the sixteenth chapter, and hold fast to stillness, and you will begin to see the world as the writer saw it. The ten thousand things rise and flourish, and then every one of them goes back to the root from which it came, just as the leaves of the forest return to the soil. There is nothing to be sad about, he implies, since it is only the way of all things.

To go back to the root is to find stillness, says the sixteenth chapter, and to know this unchanging fact is to be enlightened, while those who do not know it blunder into disaster. One who knows it becomes open-minded, and being open-minded he becomes fair, and being fair he becomes like a king, or even like heaven itself. In such a state, concludes the chapter, a person may live to the end of his life without danger.

In the seventeenth chapter the writer ranks four kinds of ruler, and the best is the one whom the people scarcely know is there at all. After him comes the ruler who is loved and praised, then the ruler who is feared, and last of all the ruler who is despised by those he governs. It is a strange kind of greatness, the author seems to say, to be great without ever being noticed at all.

Where trust is lacking, the chapter says, distrust is bound to follow, and a ruler who has made many promises will soon be found out. The good ruler is careful with his words, and when his work is done and his aims are met, the people all say that they did it themselves. He asks for no credit, and so he is never short of loyal friends.

When the great Way is forgotten, the eighteenth chapter observes dryly, people start to speak loudly of kindness and duty, as though these were things that could be taught from a book. When cleverness comes into fashion, a great deal of pretending comes with it, for people learn to look good before they learn to be good. The writer is not against goodness; he is against the noise that follows when it has gone missing.

When a family has lost its harmony, the chapter says, people begin to speak of dutiful children, and when a country falls into confusion, people begin to speak of loyal officials. These virtues are praised only because they have become rare, in the way that nobody makes a fuss about clean air until it has gone bad. The remark is a gentle warning that the loudest praise often points to the deepest lack.

Throw away cleverness and the clever schemes that go with it, says the nineteenth chapter, and the people will be a hundred times better off than before. Throw away loud talk of kindness and duty, and they will return to the natural love that families have for one another. The writer seems to say that we trip over our own good ideas, and that a little simplicity would be a great relief.

Give up the love of skill and profit, the chapter continues, and there will be no thieves left in the land, since there will be nothing worth stealing. These three ideas, however, are not enough in themselves, and so something must be offered for people to hold on to: look plain, like undyed silk, and hold fast to the simple, like uncarved wood. Care less for yourself and want little, says the writer, and a good deal of trouble will melt away.

The twentieth chapter begins with a strange line, which is that if you gave up learning you would have no worries, and then it turns into a very personal confession. Everyone else, the writer says, is feasting and laughing, as if they were climbing a terrace in the springtime, while he alone sits quietly, like a baby who has not yet learned to smile. It is the loneliest moment in the book, and also one of the most honest.

The writer goes on to say that he feels weary and drifting, like a man who has no home to return to at the end of the day. Other people have more than they could ever need, but he alone seems to have been left out, and he describes his own mind as that of a fool, quite muddled and empty. We should not take this too sadly, since the whole passage is half a joke at the expense of clever people.

Ordinary people, says the writer, appear so bright and so clear that they seem to shine, whereas he is dim and dull, as if he had been left in the shade. He is as calm as the open sea, and as free as the wind that has no place where it must come to rest. Nobody can tell whether he is boasting or complaining, and that doubt is part of the charm.

Everyone else, says the writer, has a purpose and a plan, while he remains stubborn and rustic, like a person who has never left the village. The one thing that sets him apart is that he prizes being fed by the great Mother, which is to say by the Way that gives life to all things. It is a humble claim, but it contains the whole book in a nutshell.

The twenty-first chapter says that the greatest virtue is simply to follow the Way, and to follow nothing else at all. The Way itself is vague and hard to catch, flickering in the dark like a faint light in a cave, yet inside it there are images and shapes, and at the very centre something fine and pure. It is a puzzle, the writer seems to say, that cannot be solved but can only be lived with, quietly and patiently.

The essence at the heart of the Way, the chapter insists, is quite real, and it can be trusted to be what it is. From ancient times until today its name has not been lost, and by looking through it the writer is able to watch the beginnings of all things. He asks how he knows that this is how things begin, and he answers simply that he knows it by this.

Bend, says the twenty-second chapter, and you will become whole; be crooked, and you will end by being straight; be hollow, and you will one day be filled. What is worn out becomes new, whoever has little will gain, and whoever has a great deal will be left bewildered. These sayings sound like riddles, but anyone who has watched a bamboo bend in a storm and spring back will understand them.

The sage embraces the One and in that way becomes a model for the world, says the chapter, though he never sets out to be one. Since he does not put himself on display he shines more brightly, and since he never insists that he is in the right, others come to treat him with respect. It is as if the light came from him because he was not trying to be seen.

He does not boast, and so his deeds are valued; he does not brag, and so his name endures. Because he refuses to compete with anyone, the chapter says, nobody in the whole world is able to compete with him. The old saying that those who yield will remain whole, it adds, is certainly not an empty one, for it has been proved over and over again.

Few words are natural, says the twenty-third chapter, and the proof is in the weather. A whirlwind does not blow for the whole of a morning, and a heavy downpour does not last through an entire day, because wild force burns itself out quickly. Quiet speech, like a steady drizzle, can go on for much longer without exhausting anyone.

Heaven and earth conjured up the storm, and even they cannot sustain it indefinitely, so how much less can ordinary mortals hope to maintain a display of force? The chapter says that those who follow the Way become one with the Way, and those who follow goodness are united with goodness, while those who follow loss are united with loss. Where trust is lacking, it concludes sombrely, distrust is bound to follow, for people will not trust those who have not first trusted them.

A man who stands on tiptoe in order to look taller cannot hold his balance for long, says the twenty-fourth chapter. A man who takes enormous strides in order to impress his friends cannot walk very far, because he will soon be out of breath. The picture is a comic one, and it reminds us that most of our efforts to rise above others only make us unsteady.

The person who puts himself on show, says the chapter, does not really shine, and the person who always insists he is right does not win respect. Boasting earns no true merit, and bragging cannot last, for people get tired of it very soon. It is almost the same list that appeared in the twenty-second chapter, except that this time the writer is warning us, not praising the sage.

Seen from the standpoint of the Tao, says the chapter, such habits are like scraps of leftover food or a bag of useless luggage that nobody wants to carry. Everyone finds them unpleasant, and so a person who follows the Way will not settle among them. The twenty-fourth chapter ends on this plain note, with no further explanation, as though the point had been made.

Something existed before heaven and earth were born, says the twenty-fifth chapter, something silent, formless and complete in itself. It stands alone and does not change, it moves in every direction without ever tiring, and it may well be the mother of the world. Whatever it is, it was already there, patient and unchanged, long before the first morning ever came.

I do not know its name, says the writer, and so I call it the Way, and if I am forced to give it another name, I will say that it is great. To be great means to go on, to go far, and in the end to return, like a ring of birds that sweeps out over the hills and curves back to where it began. In a few plain words the chapter has drawn a perfect circle in the air.

There are four great things in the world, says the chapter, which are the Way, heaven, earth and the king, who is counted last and with some caution. People follow the pattern of the earth, the earth follows the pattern of heaven, heaven follows the pattern of the Way, and the Way follows only what is natural. The chain ends, in other words, not with a god or a law but with the simple idea of being what one is.

What is heavy is the root of what is light, says the twenty-sixth chapter, and what is still is the master of what is restless. For this reason, the sage who travels all day long never wanders far from his heavy baggage wagon, which holds everything he really needs. His steadiness is the very thing that allows him to travel so lightly in his heart.

Though splendid sights pass before his eyes, the sage remains calm and sits quietly at home in himself. How, asks the chapter, can the lord of ten thousand chariots treat his own person lightly, rushing about the empire like a man who has forgotten something? Whoever is light-minded, the chapter concludes, loses his root, and whoever is restless in spirit loses his command.

The twenty-seventh chapter opens with a list of masters whose skill is so great that it cannot be seen. A good traveller leaves no tracks and a good speaker leaves no fault to be found, a good door has no bolt and yet cannot be opened, and a good knot uses no rope and yet cannot be untied. In each case, the best work is the work that does not announce itself.

In the same way, says the chapter, the sage is good at helping people, and for that reason he abandons no one, however poor or foolish. He is just as good at saving things, so that nothing is wasted or thrown aside as though it had no use. This habit of patient care, the writer says, is what is meant by following the light of the Way.

The good person, says the chapter, is the teacher of the person who is not yet good, and the person who is not yet good is the material on which the teacher works. Whoever does not honour the teacher, or does not care for the material, is greatly lost, however clever he may seem to be. The writer calls this the essential mystery, and it is a mystery about kindness.

Know what it is to be strong, says the twenty-eighth chapter, but hold to what is gentle, and you will become the valley into which the whole world flows. When you are such a valley, constant virtue will never leave you, and you will find your way back to the state of a small child. In the same way, one who knows what it is to be bright may choose to keep to what is dark.

Know what honour is, says the chapter, but stay content with a humble place, and you will return to the uncarved block of wood, which can still become anything. When the block is cut it turns into vessels and tools, and the sage uses these to govern, yet he knows that the greatest carving cuts very little. The block is the book's favourite picture of simplicity, a thing that is whole before anyone has decided what it should be for.

Those who want to take over the world and remake it to their own taste, says the twenty-ninth chapter, will in the end fail to do so. The world is a sacred vessel, as delicate as a clay jar, and those who try to act on it will spoil it, while those who clutch at it will drop it. A firm hand may be needed in the workshop, but it is the wrong tool for the world.

In the world, says the chapter, some people lead and others follow, some blow hot and others cold, some are strong and others weak, and some rise while others fall. Faced with all this variety, the sage avoids what is extreme, what is excessive and what is extravagant, and he keeps to a middle road. He does not try to turn everyone into the same sort of person, which is very sensible.

One who serves a ruler by the Way, says the thirtieth chapter, does not try to force the world with weapons, for such actions have a habit of returning to the one who began them. Wherever an army has camped, thorns and brambles spring up, and after a great war come the lean years, when the fields are neglected and the people go hungry. The writer's description of the aftermath is sober, and it carries no glory at all.

A good commander achieves his result and then stops, says the chapter, and he never dares to take more than he needs by force. He does not boast of his success, he does not brag about it, and he takes no pride in it, because he fought only when there was no other choice. A man who loves victory for its own sake, the author hints, is not to be trusted with an army.

When anything has reached the height of its strength, the chapter says, it has already begun to grow old, as a young bull in its prime will soon be a tired old one. Forceful growth of this sort is not in keeping with the Way, and whatever is not in keeping with the Way comes early to its end. The warning is addressed to every ruler who thinks that his strength is permanent.

Weapons are instruments of ill omen, says the thirty-first chapter, and most people feel an instinctive dislike for them. For that reason, anyone who follows the Way does not keep company with them, and the wise ruler, at home in time of peace, honours the left-hand side, the side of life. In time of war, by contrast, he honours the right, which is why the book calls war a kind of funeral.

Weapons are not the tools of a gentleman, the chapter insists, and he picks them up only when he has no other choice, and even then he prefers calm and quiet restraint. A victory, in his eyes, is never beautiful, and anyone who thinks it beautiful must enjoy killing. Whoever delights in killing, the writer concludes, will never get what he truly wants from the world.

When many people have been killed, the chapter says, they should be mourned with sorrow and tears, even by those who have won the day. A victory should therefore be marked in the same way as a funeral, with the general standing on the side of mourning and treating the winning of the battle as a grief and not a glory. It is a powerful picture, and it was written long before the modern world learned how much it needed it.

The Way is always without a name, says the thirty-second chapter, like a plain block of wood that has not yet been carved, and although it seems small, nothing in the world can master it. If kings and lords could hold fast to it, all things would come to them of their own accord, heaven and earth would join to let fall a sweet dew, and the people would live in peace without being commanded. It is a lovely picture, the sort of order that is never given by any command but simply grows by itself.

Once the block of wood has been cut up, the chapter says, names begin to appear, and then it becomes necessary to know where to stop, for the person who knows when to stop meets with no danger. The Way's place in the world is like that of the little streams in the valley, which run down toward the great rivers and the sea. Nobody has to order them to go, and nobody needs to call them back.

To know other people is to be clever, says the thirty-third chapter, but to know oneself is to be truly wise. It is much easier to study the faults of our neighbours than to look honestly at our own, and the writer seems to enjoy the small joke that this is so. Whoever has looked into the still pond of the mind and recognised the face there has already learned the hardest lesson.

To overcome other people requires force, says the chapter, but to overcome oneself requires true strength, which is a far rarer thing. A man may defeat every rival in the land and still be the slave of his own temper, his own greed or his own fear. The only battle that finally matters, the writer suggests, is the one that is fought quietly inside.

The one who knows contentment is rich, says the chapter, however small his house may be, and the one who keeps to his own proper place will endure. Even death, the writer adds, is not the end for the person who is remembered with love, since such a person has in a sense lived a very long life. Modern readers often translate this last line in different ways, and it remains one of the more puzzling of the chapter.

The great Way is like a flood that flows everywhere, says the thirty-fourth chapter, moving to the left and to the right without being asked. All things depend on it for their life, and it turns none of them away, yet when its work is done it does not put its name to it. It clothes and feeds the ten thousand things, and it does not set itself up as their master.

Since the Way is always free from desire, the chapter says, it might be called small, and since all things return to it without being ruled by it, it might equally be called great. It is a curious idea that the thing is great precisely because it never tries to be. Because it never makes itself great, the writer concludes, it is able to accomplish greatness.

Hold fast to the great image of the Way, says the thirty-fifth chapter, and the world will come to you of its own accord, as travellers come to a lantern on a dark road. They come without harm, since nobody is afraid of a person who is not grasping, and they find safety, peace and calm. A leader who is truly at rest becomes a place of rest for others.

Music and good food will make even a passing guest stop and linger, but the Way, when it is put into words, seems plain and almost without flavour. Look at it and you cannot see it, listen to it and you cannot hear it, and yet, says the thirty-fifth chapter, you can use it for ever without using it up. Its quiet, in other words, is not poverty at all but an endless and inexhaustible supply of strength.

If you want something to shrink, says the thirty-sixth chapter, first allow it to stretch out, and if you want something to grow weak, first allow it to become strong. If you wish to bring something down, you must first lift it up, and if you wish to take, you must first give. The writer calls this subtle insight, and it describes the way that every great wave rises before it falls.

The soft and the weak, says the chapter, overcome the hard and the strong, which is exactly the opposite of what most people expect. This is the quiet principle behind all the sayings that came before it, and it is a theme to which the whole book returns again and again. A green shoot that pushes through a paving stone has known it all along.

A fish ought never to leave the deep water where it is at home, says the thirty-sixth chapter, and a state ought never to put its sharpest weapons on public display. Power that is hidden is safer than power that is shown, and what is gentle and quiet is safer than what is loud. The chapter ends on this note of caution, which suits its subject exactly and leaves the reader thoughtful.

The thirty-seventh chapter closes the first half of the book, and it does so with the most famous paradox of all. The Way, it says, always does nothing, and yet nothing is left undone, just as the fields turn green and the rivers run without anyone giving an order. The thing is difficult to believe until one has watched it happen in a garden.

If kings and lords could only hold to it, says the chapter, the ten thousand things would change by themselves, in their own time and in their own way. Should desire rise up in the course of that change, the nameless uncarved block, the Way in its simplest form, would be enough to calm it. Without desire there is stillness, and in stillness the world puts itself in order without any help.

With the thirty-eighth chapter the book turns to the subject of virtue, which is the Te of its title, and it begins with a paradox. The highest virtue is not aware of itself as virtue, and for that reason it is real, whereas the lowest virtue never forgets for a moment how good it is, and for that reason it has none at all. The most generous people are often those who would be surprised to hear that they have been generous.

When the Way is lost, says the chapter, people fall back on virtue, and when virtue is lost they fall back on kindness, then on duty, and last of all on ritual. Ritual, in the writer's blunt phrase, is the thin edge of loyalty and trust and the beginning of disorder, because it is what remains after the real feeling has gone. Each step on the staircase, the writer implies, takes us a little further from the light of the Way.

Cleverness about the future, says the chapter, is only the flower of the Way and the beginning of folly, since a flower is pretty but is not food. The great person therefore lives in what is solid and not in what is thin, and he chooses the fruit rather than the flower. He leaves the one behind and takes the other, in the quiet confidence that what is real will outlast what is merely pleasing.

In the beginning, says the thirty-ninth chapter, there were certain things that attained the One, which is another name for the unity of the Way. Heaven attained it and became clear, the earth attained it and became steady, the spirits attained it and became powerful, and the valleys attained it and became full. The rulers attained it too, and by it they became the upright guides of the world.

Without clarity, the chapter says, heaven would soon crack, and without steadiness, the earth would split open like a dry riverbed. The spirits would fade away if they lost their power, the valleys would run dry if they ceased to be full, and the rulers would fall if they ceased to be upright. Everything, in other words, depends on keeping hold of the one thing that holds all things together.

The noble have the humble as their root, says the chapter, and the high rest upon the low, which is why rulers once called themselves by such modest names as the lonely, the orphan and the unworthy. Take a carriage apart, the writer adds, and count every wheel, axle and board, and you will have counted the parts without having found a carriage, a line that many translators read in different ways. The author does not wish to tinkle like a precious piece of jade, but to be as plain and solid as a stone.

Returning is the movement of the Tao, says the fortieth chapter, and yielding is the way in which it works, like a ripple that spreads over a pond and slowly dies away into calm. The whole of the book's wisdom seems to be folded into these few words, which say that what goes out must come back, and that what is soft is the true power. It is among the shortest of all the chapters, and many readers find it among the deepest.

All the ten thousand things of the world, the chapter says, are born from being, which is to say from what can be seen and touched. That being is born in its turn from non-being, from the quiet and formless ground that cannot be seen at all, as a seed sprouts in dark soil that nobody can see into. The chapter ends here, leaving the reader to sit for a moment with the thought.

When the best kind of student hears of the Way, says the forty-first chapter, he sets out at once to practise it with all his strength. The middling student keeps it for a while and then forgets it, but the lowest kind of student simply bursts out laughing. The writer adds with a smile that if the lowest did not laugh, it would not be the Way, since a teaching that nobody laughs at is probably too ordinary to be true.

The chapter quotes a list of old sayings, each of which turns an expectation upside down. The bright Way seems dark, the advancing Way seems to be retreating, and the smooth Way seems rough, while the highest virtue is like an empty valley. In every case the true thing wears the face of its opposite, so that appearances are never to be trusted.

The great square has no corners, the chapter goes on, the great vessel takes the longest time to finish, the great sound is faint to the ear, and the great image has no shape at all. The Way is hidden, and it has no name, yet it alone is good at nourishing all things and bringing them to completion. The finest things, it seems, can neither be rushed nor be pointed at, and perhaps that is why they last.

The Tao gave birth to one, says the forty-second chapter, and one gave birth to two, and two gave birth to three, and three gave birth to all the ten thousand things of the world. Readers have argued for centuries about what these numbers stand for, and nobody can say for sure. The picture is simple enough to enjoy without an answer, like one flame that lights a lamp, and then a whole hall of lamps.

All the ten thousand things, says the chapter, carry yin on their backs and embrace yang in their arms, which is to say the dark and the light, the soft and the hard, the still and the moving. By blending these two kinds of energy, which the book calls breath, they come into harmony with each other. Neither partner wins, and the world is what is left when they are balanced.

People hate to be called lonely, orphaned or unworthy, the chapter remarks, and yet kings and lords once chose these very names for themselves, as a way of staying humble. In the same way, things are sometimes increased by being decreased and decreased by being increased, which is another of the book's gentle paradoxes. The writer also teaches what others have taught, that the violent are unlikely to die a natural death.

The softest thing in the world, says the forty-third chapter, gallops over the hardest, as water wears a hollow in the grey rock over many years. What has no substance at all can enter even a place that has no crack or space, and this, the writer says, is how he knows the value of not forcing. It is the lesson of the river and the stone, put in the fewest possible words.

Teaching without words, says the chapter, and acting without forcing, are of a value that few people in the world are able to reach. The teacher who sits quietly beside a student, saying nothing, may pass on more than the teacher who talks for an hour. It is an old and rather inconvenient truth, since silence is so much harder to practise than speech.

Which is dearer to you, asks the forty-fourth chapter, your good name or your own self, and which matters more, your own self or all your wealth? It also asks which is the worse, gaining or losing, and it leaves each reader to answer in private. The questions are meant to be uncomfortable, since most of us spend our lives behaving as if fame and wealth were the dearer things.

Great love, says the chapter, comes at a great cost, and a great store of goods brings the heavy loss that goes with it, since the more we pile up, the more there is to fear for. The one who knows contentment is never disgraced, and the one who knows when to stop is never in danger, and such a person can go on living for a very long time. It is perhaps the most practical piece of advice in the whole book, and certainly one of the easiest to try.

Great perfection, says the forty-fifth chapter, looks as though it had a flaw in it, and yet it is never worn out by use. Great fullness looks like emptiness, and yet it never runs dry, like an old dented kettle that has served tea to a thousand guests and still has more to give. The wise know that a thing which looks too perfect is usually only new.

Great straightness seems bent, says the chapter, and great skill looks clumsy to the eye that expects show. Great eloquence seems to stammer, because the best speaker has no need to impress anyone and simply says what he means, a little slowly, in plain words. The master carpenter, in the same way, may work with the plainest tools and make the least noise.

Movement overcomes the cold, says the chapter, and stillness overcomes the heat, as every traveller knows who has walked fast on a winter morning or rested in the shade at noon. In the same way, a mind that is clear and quiet is able to set the standard by which everything else is measured. The chapter ends here, on the idea that peace of mind is the true level of the world.

When the Way prevails in the world, says the forty-sixth chapter, the swiftest horses are put to the plough and used to haul manure for the fields. When the Way is absent, war horses are bred on the borders of the country, where the farms once stood, and the young men are taken to be soldiers. The two pictures show how a whole land can change according to what it prizes.

There is no greater misfortune, says the chapter, than not knowing when you have enough, and there is no greater fault than the wish to take more than you need. The man who is content with what he has is always satisfied, whereas the man who is never satisfied will be hungry at the richest feast. The contentment of knowing that enough is enough, concludes the writer, is a contentment that never runs out.

Without stepping out of the door, says the forty-seventh chapter, a person may come to know the whole world, and without looking out of the window, he may see the Way of heaven. This is not an argument for laziness but for depth, since the most important truths are often found by looking inward and not by looking farther. It is a bold claim from a book written in an age when long journeys were rare.

The farther a person travels, the less he may come to know, says the chapter, since distance without understanding is only a longer way of being lost. The sage, by contrast, knows without having to go anywhere, understands what things are without needing to see them, and accomplishes his aims without any forced action. The writer is not against travel, only against the idea that travel is a substitute for wisdom.

In the pursuit of learning, says the forty-eighth chapter, something is gained every day, and the scholar's desk grows heavier with books. In the pursuit of the Way, something is dropped every day, and the seeker's life grows lighter and clearer, like a garden from which the weeds have been pulled. The two kinds of knowing are not enemies, but they point in opposite directions.

Less and less is done, says the chapter, until at last one arrives at doing nothing, and when nothing is forced, nothing is left undone. A gardener who has planted well and watered well may sit down in the shade and watch his garden grow without lifting a finger. The writer does not recommend idleness; he recommends the kind of work that has no strain in it.

The world is always won by not meddling, says the chapter, and the best rulers have understood this for as long as there have been rulers. Whoever begins to interfere in every small matter, and to make a rule for each new problem, is not fit to rule the world at all. The thought is a pointed one in a book that, according to the legend, was written for a gatekeeper and meant to be read by kings.

The sage has no fixed mind of his own, says the forty-ninth chapter, and he does not cling to his opinions as a rock clings to the shore. He takes the hearts of the people as his own heart, listening to what they need before he decides what to do. A leader who has already made up his mind about everything has nothing left to learn from the ones he leads.

To those who are good I am good, says the sage in the forty-ninth chapter, and to those who are not good I am also good, because goodness is the very nature of virtue. To those who are faithful I am faithful, and to those who are not faithful I am faithful too, so that trust grows where it was lacking. It is a hard teaching to carry out, but a simple one to understand.

The sage lives in the world with great care, says the chapter, and he blends his own mind with the mind of everyone around him, without making a show of it. The people fix their eyes and ears on him and wait to see what he will do, and he looks upon them all as a kindly parent looks upon children. It is a picture of leadership that has more to do with listening than with command.

Going out into the world is life, says the fiftieth chapter, and coming in again is death, and between the two lies the whole of human experience. Of every ten people, the writer says, some are followers of life, some are followers of death, and some are living people who walk toward their own deaths by the way that they live. Translators read the numbers in this passage in different ways, and the chapter is more a riddle than a rule, so a reader should not take it too literally.

Why does this happen, the writer asks, and he answers that it is because those people hold on to life too tightly, as a man clutches a bag of gold on a dangerous road. They treat every day as an emergency, and in their effort to protect life they use up the very life that they are trying to protect. Those who relax their grip, he implies, are the ones who live longest and best.

The one who knows how to live well, says the writer, can walk through the hills without meeting a tiger or a wild buffalo, and can pass through a battle without being touched by a weapon. The wild buffalo finds no place to drive its horn, the tiger finds no place to set its claws, and the soldier finds no place to thrust his blade. The reason, the chapter says, is that such a person has no place in him where death can enter.

The Way gives birth to all things, says the fifty-first chapter, and virtue feeds them, while the world gives them shape and circumstance brings them to completion. Because of this, the ten thousand things honour the Way and prize virtue, though nobody has ever commanded them to do so, since such honour is always free and always natural. A seedling in the sun does not need to be told whom to thank.

The Way gives birth to things and then feeds them, brings them up, shelters them, matures them and protects them as a bird protects its young beneath her wing. It produces without possessing, it acts without relying on its own acts, and it leads without ever trying to control, and the book calls this its mysterious virtue. This line appears nearly word for word in the tenth chapter, which suggests how much the writer valued it.

The world had a beginning, says the fifty-second chapter, and that beginning may be called the mother of the world. If we know the mother, we can know her children, and once we know the children we can return to hold the mother, so that when our own lives end, we are not in danger. The writer is speaking of the Way in the language of the family, which is perhaps the warmest language that he has.

Block the openings of the senses, says the chapter, and close the doors, and you will not be troubled for the whole of your life. Open them wide and become involved in endless business, and no one will be able to help you, but to see what is small is clarity, and to keep to what is soft is strength. Use the light, then return to the clarity within, and in this way you will practise what the writer calls constancy.

If I had even a little knowledge, says the writer of the fifty-third chapter, I would walk upon the great Way, and I would fear only that I might stray from it. The great Way is smooth and level, but people are strangely fond of the narrow side paths, with their shortcuts, their views and their promises. It is as if a traveller on a fine road were to prefer the ditch.

The palaces are spotless, says the chapter, but the fields are choked with weeds and the storehouses are empty, while the rulers dress in fine clothes, carry sharp swords and feast until they are stuffed. They have more wealth than they could ever use, and the writer calls this the splendour of robbers, which has nothing whatever to do with the Way. It is the sharpest social criticism in the whole book, and it is aimed at the very people who might have read it.

What is well planted cannot be pulled up, says the fifty-fourth chapter, and what is well held cannot slip away, just as an old tree with deep roots stands firm when the wind comes down the valley. In the same way, the children and grandchildren of someone who has built on a sound foundation will honour his memory for generation after generation. The chapter is talking about virtue, which, like a tree, has to be planted before it can be harvested.

Cultivate virtue in your own person, says the chapter, and it will become real, and cultivate it in your family, and it will grow richer with each year. Cultivate it in the village, and it will last, cultivate it in the country, and it will flourish, and cultivate it in the whole world, and it will spread to every corner of it. The pattern is the same as a lamp that lights one room, then a house, then a street, and then a town.

Therefore, says the chapter, look at a person by the measure of one person, at a family by the measure of one family, and at a village or a country in the same way. Look at the whole world by the measure of the whole world, and you will find that the same pattern repeats at every size. How do I know that this is how the world is, asks the writer, and he answers briefly that he knows it by this.

One who is rich in virtue, says the fifty-fifth chapter, may be compared to a newborn child, which has no enemies because it has no wish to harm anyone. Stinging insects do not sting such a child, wild beasts do not seize it, and birds of prey do not swoop down on it. The writer is not telling us that this is literally true, but that gentleness is a kind of protection.

The bones of a newborn child are soft and its muscles are weak, says the chapter, and yet its grip is surprisingly firm, so that it holds on to a finger with all its strength. It can cry all day long and never become hoarse, and the writer takes this as a sign of perfect harmony, a life that is not at war with itself. Anyone who has held a baby will have felt the truth of the picture.

To know harmony, says the chapter, is to know the constant, and to know the constant is to be enlightened, whereas to force life along is a bad omen, and to make the mind drive the breath is only strain. Whatever grows strong too quickly will soon begin to age, which is not the Way, and whatever is not the Way comes early to its end. The chapter repeats a line from the thirtieth, as if to remind the reader of a lesson that is easily forgotten.

Those who know do not speak, says the fifty-sixth chapter, and those who speak do not know, which is a fine saying and a rather uncomfortable one for a book to quote. Some readers have smiled at the fact that the writer used about five thousand written characters to tell us that words fall short. The point is not that we should never speak, but that what matters most cannot be handed over in a sentence.

Block the openings, says the chapter, blunt what is sharp, untie what is tangled, soften the glare and merge with the dust, and you will reach what is called mysterious sameness. A person who has reached it cannot be drawn close or pushed away, cannot be helped or harmed, and cannot be raised up or brought low. For this very reason, the chapter concludes, the world treasures him above all others, as it treasures a quiet spring in the hills.

Rule a country by being straight with its people, says the fifty-seventh chapter, and wage a war by taking the enemy by surprise, as the old generals taught. But if you want to win the whole world, the writer says, you must do it by not meddling in the lives of ordinary people. The first two rules are the usual ones in every textbook of kings, and the third is the book's own.

The more prohibitions there are in the world, says the chapter, the poorer the people become, and the more sharp weapons the people have, the greater the confusion in the land. The more cleverness there is among them, the more strange things appear, and the more laws and orders are posted on the walls, the more thieves there will be. The writer evidently believed that a good society is not made by adding to its rules.

The sage therefore says that if he does nothing, the people will change of their own accord, and that if he loves stillness, they will become upright. If he does not meddle in their affairs they will prosper by their own work, and if he has no desires of his own, they will return to a simple and honest way of life. It is a very bold promise, and nobody has ever tried it on a large scale.

When the government is quiet and seems rather dull, says the fifty-eighth chapter, the people are simple and honest in their dealings with one another. When the government is sharp and prying, always asking questions and always looking over shoulders, the people become crafty and learn to hide what they do. Suspicion, in other words, tends to produce in the end the very dishonesty that it was meant to prevent.

Misfortune is what good fortune leans upon, says the chapter, and good fortune is the place in which misfortune lies hidden, like a coin that has two faces. Who can say how things will end, the writer asks, for there is no fixed standard by which to measure it. What looks like the right course may turn out to be strange, and what looks like a blessing may turn out to be a trial.

The sage is square, says the chapter, but he does not cut anyone with his corners; he is sharp but he does not pierce, and he is straight without being rigid. He is bright, but his brightness does not dazzle those around him, and so people feel at ease in his presence. It is a portrait of a person who has strong principles and soft manners.

In governing people and in serving heaven, says the fifty-ninth chapter, there is nothing as good as frugality, which means taking only what is needed and keeping the rest in store. It means preparing early, as a farmer fills his granary before the winter, and preparing early means gathering virtue, until at last nothing is beyond reach. Frugality, in this sense, is less a matter of money than a matter of not wasting oneself or one's energy.

When nothing is beyond a person's reach, the chapter says, nobody can see his limit, and he is fit to take care of a whole country. The one who holds the mother of the country, that is, the Way itself, will last a long time, and this is what the writer calls having deep roots and a firm base. It is the way to a long life and a lasting vision, and it is open to anyone with the patience to put down roots.

Ruling a large country, says the sixtieth chapter, is like cooking a small fish, and anyone who has ever fried one will see at once what the writer means. If you prod it, turn it and fuss over it, it falls to pieces in the pan, and the dinner is ruined. The saying has become one of the most quoted in the whole book, and it is still repeated by people who have never read anything else in it.

When the world is ruled by the Way, says the chapter, the spirits of the dead lose their power to harm, not because the power has vanished, but because it is no longer turned against the living. Neither the spirits nor the sage do any harm to the people, and so the goodness of both comes back to them. A peaceful country, the writer suggests, is one in which nobody is afraid of the night.

A great country, says the sixty-first chapter, ought to be like the low ground at the bottom of a valley, the place downstream where all the rivers of the world come together. In the writer's language it is the female of the world, which wins by being quiet and by lying low, in the same way that a wide plain gathers all the streams that run down from the hills. Its power lies in what it receives, says the writer, and not in anything that it takes by force from others.

A big country that is humble before a small one, says the chapter, will win the trust of the small country, and a small country that is humble before a big one will gain the protection of the big country. Some countries lower themselves in order to win, and some lower themselves and are taken over, so the writer is careful to say what each kind of humility is for. The wisdom of the passage is that politeness between neighbours is usually cheaper than war.

The big country, says the chapter, wishes to unite and to feed more people than its own, while the small country only wishes to join in and be of service to someone strong. Each of them may get what it wants, but since the big one has so much more to lose from pride, it is the big one that should be the first to lower itself. This chapter shows the book at its most practical, applying its gentle teaching to the quarrels between nations.

The Way is the hidden shelter of the ten thousand things, says the sixty-second chapter, a quiet place which nobody built and which nobody can lock. It is the treasure of the good person, and also the refuge of the person who is not good, who may take shelter there without having to explain. Fine words can win a person honour in the market, the writer admits, and good deeds can raise him above others, but even if someone is not good, why should he be thrown away?

When an emperor is crowned and his three ministers are appointed, says the chapter, people bring them jade discs and carriages drawn by teams of four horses, which are the finest gifts in the land. It would be better, the writer thinks, to sit quietly and offer them the Way, which cannot be stolen or worn out. The ancients prized it, he adds, because by means of it the seeker finds, and the person who has done wrong may be forgiven, and for that reason it is the treasure of the world.

Act without acting, says the sixty-third chapter, work without fuss, and learn to taste what has no taste, which is to find a quiet flavour in plain things. Whether the matter is large or small, whether the injuries are many or few, the writer advises that hatred should be answered with virtue. It is a line that people have often compared to other great traditions, though the book itself makes no such comparison.

Plan for the difficult while it is still easy, says the chapter, and do the great while it is still small, for all the hardest tasks in the world begin with something easy. The sage never sets out to do anything grand, and that is why he manages to achieve greatness in the end. Whoever promises lightly keeps few promises, and whoever treats every task as easy will meet many difficulties, and so the sage takes everything seriously and has no difficulties at all.

What is at rest is easy to hold, says the sixty-fourth chapter, and what has not yet shown any sign is easy to plan for. What is brittle is easy to break, and what is tiny is easy to scatter, so deal with a thing before it exists, and put the house in order before the disorder begins. A farmer who mends a crack in a dam with a handful of clay has saved himself a great deal of effort afterwards, and that is the chapter's whole lesson.

A tree that is as thick as a man's embrace, says the chapter, grew from a tiny sprout, and a tower of nine storeys began as a small heap of earth. A journey of a thousand miles starts from beneath one's feet, which is the most famous line in the whole book and one of the most quoted sayings in the world. Every great thing, the chapter reminds us, has to begin with a very small one, and often with a single step.

Those who force things spoil them, says the chapter, and those who grasp at things lose them, while the sage who does not force or grasp neither spoils nor loses. People often fail when a task is almost finished, and so, the writer says, one should be as careful at the end as at the beginning. The sage desires not to desire, he does not prize rare goods, and he helps the ten thousand things to follow their own nature without daring to push them.

Those who followed the Way in ancient times, says the sixty-fifth chapter, did not try to make the people cunning, but kept them simple and open-hearted. Translators differ on how harshly to put this, and it is best read as a warning against scheming and not against learning. People are hard to rule, says the writer, when they are full of clever plans.

To rule a country by cleverness, says the chapter, is to do it harm, and to rule it without cleverness is to do it good. Whoever knows these two things has found a model, and whoever keeps the model always in mind has what the book calls mysterious virtue, which is deep and far-reaching. It goes out with all things and returns with them, like a river, until at last it arrives at great harmony.

Rivers and seas, says the sixty-sixth chapter, are the kings of the hundred valleys, and the reason is that they are good at being lower than the valleys that feed them. Every stream runs down to them without being called, and every drop of rain ends up in their keeping, since a low place is a place of welcome. The picture is a gentle one, but it has the force of a law of nature.

The sage who wishes to stand above the people, says the chapter, must put himself below them in the way that he speaks, and the one who wishes to lead them must walk behind them. A leader who is always shouting from the front is soon out of sight, while the one at the back can see who is tired and who has fallen behind. It is a lesson that the best teachers and the best captains have always known.

In this way the sage stands above the people, and they do not feel the weight of him, and he walks in front of them, and they are not hurt by his coming. The whole world delights in pushing him forward and never grows tired of doing so, because he does not compete with anyone. Since he does not compete, says the writer, nobody in the world is able to compete with him.

Everyone in the world says that my Way is great, says the writer of the sixty-seventh chapter, but that it seems unlike anything else, and he replies that this is exactly why it is great. If it were like anything in the world, he points out, it would long ago have become small and ordinary. He then says that he has three treasures which he holds and keeps, the first being compassion, the second being frugality, and the third being never to put himself first in the world.

Because I am compassionate, says the writer, I can afford to be brave, and because I am frugal, I can afford to be generous with others. Because I do not dare to put myself first in the world, I am able to become the leader of tools, which is to say the leader of those who do the work. The three treasures, therefore, do not make a person weaker, but give him the means to be strong.

People today give up compassion and try to be brave, says the chapter, give up frugality and try to be generous, and give up humility and try to be first, which can lead only to death. Compassion, on the other hand, wins the battle when it attacks and stands firm when it defends, and heaven will rescue and protect the one who has it. The idea is a surprising one for a book that is often read by soldiers.

A good warrior is not warlike, says the sixty-eighth chapter, and a good fighter is not angry, and a good conqueror does not hurry to meet the enemy in battle. A good employer of other people puts himself below them, and the writer treats all of this as part of a single idea, which is that real strength has no need of display. The calm captain, we might say, is a good deal harder to defeat than the loud one ever was.

This quality, says the chapter, is called the virtue of not competing, and it consists in using the strength of other people without trying to overpower them. It matches the way of heaven, which the writer calls the ancient ultimate, in the sense that nothing has been found that can surpass it. Two workers who carry a heavy beam together, one at each end, have understood it better than any general.

There is a saying among strategists, according to the sixty-ninth chapter, that one should not dare to be the host who starts the quarrel, but should rather be the guest who answers it. One should not dare to advance an inch, but should be ready to retreat a foot, since a general who is never in a hurry is seldom caught off balance. Even in the old manuals of war, the writer implies, patience was counted a virtue.

This, says the chapter, is what is meant by marching where there is no road, rolling up one's sleeves where there is no arm to show, and seizing where there is no weapon to hold. It means confronting an opponent who is, in a sense, not there at all, since the one who does not fight leaves nothing for the other to push against. The language is deliberately paradoxical, and it is meant to be turned over slowly in the mind.

There is no greater calamity, says the chapter, than to think lightly of the enemy, for doing so very nearly costs one all three of the treasures. When two armies meet on equal terms, the one that feels sorrow at the thought of fighting is the one that will win. The idea is not that sorrow is a weapon, but that those who take no pleasure in war are the least likely to be careless in it.

My words are very easy to understand, says the writer of the seventieth chapter, and they are very easy to put into practice. Yet nobody in the whole world seems able to understand them, and still less to practise them, and the old man's sadness is plain in his voice. It is one of the few places where the author steps out from behind his sayings and speaks about himself.
