My words have an ancestor, says the writer, and my deeds have a master, by which he means that everything he says comes from one deep source. It is only because people do not know that source that they do not know him either, and so they take his sayings for riddles. The reader is left to guess what the ancestor is, but it is not hard to guess that it is the Way.

Those who truly know me are few, says the writer, and for that reason those who follow me are honoured. The sage therefore wears coarse clothes, in the manner of an ordinary peasant, but inside his coat he carries a precious piece of jade. His value, like the jade, cannot be seen by those who look only at the surface.

To know that you do not know is the best state, says the seventy-first chapter, and not to know that you do not know is a kind of sickness. Many readers have recalled that the Greek philosopher Socrates is famously said to have held a very similar view, although there is no evidence that the two traditions ever met. The thought seems to be one of those that human beings arrive at in several different places.

Only by being sick of the sickness, says the chapter, can a person finally be free of it, which is a play on words that translates only roughly into English. The sage is not sick in this way, because he has grown weary of it, and so he has put the weight of false knowledge down at the side of the road. After that, the writer implies, a person may walk on through life much more lightly and with much less fear.

When people no longer fear a ruler's power, says the seventy-second chapter, something far greater than that power arrives, which is their anger. So the wise ruler does not make their homes narrow, and does not make their living hard, and only by not oppressing the people will he avoid being oppressed in turn. This is a warning, and it is also an old and practical piece of political advice.

So the sage knows himself, says the chapter, but he does not put himself on show, and he loves himself, but he does not think himself above anybody else. He leaves the one way of behaving behind, and takes up the other, and the choice lies between display and quiet worth. It is a very small piece of advice, but a very difficult one to follow when the world is looking.

A man who is brave in daring, says the seventy-third chapter, will sooner or later meet his end, while a man who is brave in not daring will live to see another day. Of these two kinds of bravery, one brings benefit and the other brings harm, and the writer leaves it to us to decide which is which. It is the old lesson that a rash person often mistakes recklessness for courage.

Who can say why heaven dislikes what it dislikes, asks the chapter, since even the sage finds this difficult to know. The Way of heaven does not strive, and yet it is good at winning; it does not speak, and yet it is good at answering. It does not call, yet things come to it, and it seems slow, though its plans are well made, so it is an example to anyone who is in a hurry.

Heaven's net is vast, says the chapter, and although its mesh is coarse, so that it seems to let almost everything pass, nothing in the end slips through it. The saying is both a comfort and a warning, for it declares that the great pattern of things is patient and that it overlooks no one. People have repeated it for more than two thousand years, in times of injustice, as a hope.

If people do not fear death, says the seventy-fourth chapter, then it is no use trying to frighten them with the threat of it. A ruler who relies on punishment has already lost the trust of the people, and a ruler who has lost their trust has very little left to rule with. The remark is aimed at harsh governments, and it is among the book's most direct political statements.

The chapter says that nature, or heaven, has its own master executioner, and that for a ruler to take its place is like a young man trying to carve wood in place of a master carpenter. Those who attempt such work, the writer observes, rarely escape without hurting their own hands. It is a gentle way of saying that human beings should not play the part of heaven.

People go hungry, says the seventy-fifth chapter, because their rulers eat up too much of what they grow in taxes, and for that reason the people are discontented. They are also hard to rule, the writer says, because their rulers keep on interfering with the way they live. The cause, in both cases, is to be found at the top, and not among the people.

People take death lightly, says the chapter, because they struggle so hard to hold on to life, and a person who has no peace in living has little to lose in dying. Someone who does not strive after life with such anxiety, the writer adds, is wiser than someone who prizes it too highly. It is a puzzling thought, though it is closer to calm than to despair.

When a person is born, says the seventy-sixth chapter, his body is soft and supple, and when he dies, it is hard and stiff. In the same way, the ten thousand plants and trees are soft and tender while they are alive, and dry and brittle when they are dead, like a willow in spring beside a snapped branch from last winter. It is one of the most simple and most convincing arguments in the book.

So the hard and the stiff, says the chapter, are the companions of death, and the soft and the weak are the companions of life. The proof is in every garden and every forest, where the stiff branch snaps and the springy reed bends and recovers, and where it is gentleness that lasts. Softness, in this book, is never a weakness but a way of staying alive.

An army that has grown too strong will not win, says the chapter, and a tree that has grown too strong is the first to be cut down by the woodcutter. The strong and the big take the lower place in the end, while the soft and the weak rise above them. The chapter closes with a warning, which is that no ruler should mistake the show of force for the secret of power.

The Way of heaven, says the seventy-seventh chapter, is like the drawing of a bow, in which the high part is pressed down and the low part is lifted until the arrow is level. If the string is too long, some of it is taken away, and if it is too short, something is added to it. The archer's adjustment is a picture of balance, and the chapter says that heaven keeps the world in balance in the same way.

The Way of heaven, says the chapter, reduces what is too much and makes up what is too little. But the way of people is just the opposite, for it takes from those who have too little in order to serve those who already have too much. Only one who has the Way, says the writer, can give his surplus to the world, and so the sage acts without relying on his work, for he does not wish to show his worth.

Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, says the seventy-eighth chapter, and yet when it comes to wearing away what is hard and strong, nothing can do the work better. A waterfall smooths the rock over which it falls, and a quiet stream can carve a canyon, given enough time. Nothing, the writer says, can replace it, because there is no other way of being so strong while seeming so mild.

The weak overcome the strong, and the soft overcome the hard, says the chapter, and everybody in the world knows it, although hardly anyone acts on it. The sage therefore says that whoever takes on the disgrace of his country is fit to be its lord, and whoever takes on its misfortunes is fit to be king of the world. True words, as the writer remarks, often seem to say the opposite of what we expect, and this is one of them.

After a great quarrel has been settled, says the seventy-ninth chapter, some bitterness is always left behind, and one may well ask how that can be called good. The sage therefore holds the left half of the contract, like a lender who has his tally, but he does not press the debtor for what is owed. A person of virtue attends to what he owes, and a person without virtue attends to collecting, and the Way of heaven has no favourites, though it is always with the good.

Let a country be small, says the eightieth chapter, and let its people be few, so that even if they have tools that could do the work of ten or a hundred men, they do not use them. The people take life seriously and so do not wander far from their homes, and though they own boats and carriages, nobody rides in them, and though they own armour and weapons, nobody parades them. The picture is an old dream of simplicity, and not a plan that the writer expected to be carried out.

Let the people go back to keeping their records on knotted cords, says the chapter, and let them find their food sweet, their clothes beautiful, their homes peaceful and their customs happy. Their neighbouring country is so near that the crowing of its roosters and the barking of its dogs can be heard across the border, and yet the people grow old and die without ever going there. Few readers have found it easy to decide whether this is a lovely picture or a rather sad one.

True words are not beautiful, says the eighty-first chapter, and beautiful words are not always true, a warning that applies even to the book that contains them. Good people do not argue, and those who love an argument are seldom good, and those who really know are not always widely read, while those who are widely read do not always know. These are the last sayings of the book, and they come back to the question of words with which it began.

The sage does not hoard, says the last chapter, and the more he does for other people, the more he seems to have himself, and the more he gives, the more he gains. The Way of heaven benefits all things and does not harm them, and the way of the sage is to act and not to compete. With these two quiet sentences, the book comes to its close, as gently as it began, and without any final claim.

An old story tells that Laozi grew tired of the world, rode toward the western pass on an ox, and wrote his book for the gatekeeper who begged him to leave some wisdom behind. That story was written down centuries after Laozi is said to have lived, and historians cannot say whether he was one person, several, or a name for an older tradition. What no one doubts is that this small book is among the most translated in the world, and that readers in every age have found in it a reason to slow down.
